prompt: An administrator is ordering four new rack servers that will run a commercial hypervisor under a vendor support contract. The support agreement only covers configurations the hypervisor vendor has certified. What should the administrator check before placing the order?

options.text: The hypervisor vendor's HCL for the server model, CPU and storage controller
The server manufacturer's warranty terms and the length of its on-site support window
The hypervisor's minimum RAM and CPU core count published in its installation guide
A memory diagnostic run on a loaner unit of the same model

explanation: A hardware compatibility list (HCL) shows which server models and components the software vendor has tested and will support, so it is what decides support eligibility. Minimum RAM and core counts only say the software will install, not that the hardware is certified. Warranty terms cover the hardware vendor, not hypervisor support. A memory diagnostic proves one unit is stable but says nothing about certification.

prompt: A server currently has eight 32 GB RDIMMs installed. A technician finds four spare 32 GB UDIMMs of the same speed in inventory and wants to use them to expand memory. What should the administrator tell the technician?

options.text: Install them in the remaining slots, because modules of equal speed and capacity always work together
Install them only in the second CPU's channels, one type per CPU
Install them and lower the memory speed in firmware, because UDIMMs only need a slower clock to work
Do not install them; RDIMMs and UDIMMs cannot be mixed, so order matching RDIMMs

explanation: Server platforms do not support mixing registered (RDIMM) and unbuffered (UDIMM) modules in the same system, and the board will typically fail POST or refuse the memory. Equal speed and capacity do not make different module types compatible. Splitting the types between processors is still mixing them in one system. Lowering the memory clock does not change the electrical buffering difference between the two types.

prompt: A database server runs month-end financial calculations. The business wants the memory subsystem to detect and correct single-bit errors automatically instead of silently returning bad data. Which memory feature meets this requirement?

options.text: Dual-rank memory
Higher-speed DIMMs
Non-ECC unbuffered memory
ECC memory

explanation: Error-correcting code (ECC) memory stores extra check bits so it can correct single-bit errors and detect multi-bit errors. Dual-rank describes how the DRAM chips on a module are organised and adds no error correction. Non-ECC memory has no check bits, so a flipped bit goes unnoticed. Faster DIMMs improve bandwidth but do nothing to detect or correct errors.

prompt: A memory vendor lists two 64 GB server modules with otherwise identical specifications: one labelled 1Rx4 and one labelled 2Rx4. What does the difference in the labels describe?

options.text: The number of error-correction bits per word, so a 2R module can correct double-bit memory errors
Whether the module is registered (2R) or unbuffered (1R)
The number of ranks, which are sets of DRAM chips the controller accesses as one block
The number of memory channels the module can occupy, so a 2R module uses two channels at the same time

explanation: The 1R and 2R prefix gives the number of ranks; a dual-rank module has two sets of chips that the controller addresses separately, and the x4 is the width of each DRAM chip. A module always sits in one channel. Ranks do not change how many error-correction bits a word has. Rank count is unrelated to whether a module is registered or unbuffered.

prompt: An administrator installs a passively cooled data center GPU into a 2U server to run an inference workload. Under load the GPU throttles and then shuts down because of high temperature, although the server's fans are working. The server model is not listed in the GPU vendor's support matrix. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The GPU is in a PCIe slot with too few lanes, so it draws more power
The GPU needs a separate graphics driver from the OS vendor before its fans start spinning under load
The server is not qualified for the GPU, and its airflow cannot cool a fanless card
The server firmware disabled Secure Boot for the add-in card, which forces the GPU into a thermal safe mode

explanation: Passively cooled data center GPUs have no fans of their own and depend on the server delivering enough airflow, which is why the server must be on the GPU's qualified list. A passive card has no fans for a driver to start. Fewer PCIe lanes reduce bandwidth, not power draw. Secure Boot governs signed boot code and has nothing to do with GPU thermal behaviour.

prompt: An administrator replaces the processors in a two-socket server with a newer generation from the same family. The server's documentation says the board supports that generation, but the system now fails to complete POST. What should the administrator do first?

options.text: Clear the CMOS settings and reinstall the new processors, because the old CPU settings block the newer chips
Reseat the new processors with fresh thermal paste, because poor contact stops POST before memory is tested
Replace all memory with faster RDIMMs that the new processors require
Reinstall the old CPUs and update the firmware to a release that supports the new ones

explanation: Support for a newer CPU generation usually arrives in a later BIOS/UEFI release, so the server must run that firmware before it can initialise the new chips, and the old CPUs are needed to boot it long enough to flash. Clearing CMOS does not add microcode support. Poor thermal contact causes overheating under load, not an immediate POST failure. Newer processors normally run slower supported memory at its rated speed rather than refusing to POST.

prompt: A technician installs four new SAS drives in a server's front bays, but the RAID controller does not detect them. The server's specification sheet says the drive cage has a SATA backplane. What is the cause?

options.text: The controller only detects new drives after the server is cold booted with the drives already installed
A SATA backplane cannot host SAS drives; a SAS backplane accepts both SAS and SATA drives
SAS drives must be installed in pairs on separate backplanes before the controller can see them
SAS drives need a firmware update on the drive before any backplane will power them up

explanation: SAS connectors are keyed so SATA drives fit SAS backplanes, but SAS drives do not work on a SATA-only backplane or controller. A drive firmware update would not change the backplane's interface. There is no requirement to install SAS drives in pairs across backplanes. Hot-plug capable controllers detect new drives without a cold boot, and a reboot would not fix the interface mismatch anyway.

prompt: A small accounting office with eight employees needs its first on-premises file server. The office has no server room or rack, and the server will sit under a desk in a shared workspace. Which form factor is the best fit?

options.text: Blade server
Hyperconverged appliance
Tower server
2U rack server

explanation: A tower server stands on its own, needs no rack and is usually quieter, which suits a small office without a server room. A blade needs a powered blade chassis, which is far more than eight users need. A 2U rack server is designed to be mounted in a rack and is typically loud. A hyperconverged appliance is a multi-node cluster platform, oversized and costly for one small file server.

prompt: A data center has limited rack space and power. A company needs to deploy 30 compute nodes that share power supplies, cooling fans and network switching inside a common enclosure. Which form factor meets this requirement?

options.text: Blade servers in a blade chassis
2U rack servers with shared storage
Tower servers converted with rack kits
1U rack servers with redundant PSUs

explanation: Blade servers slide into a chassis that provides shared power, cooling and network modules, giving high density in little rack space. 1U rack servers are dense but each carries its own power supplies, fans and network cabling. Tower servers converted for racks are less dense, not more. 2U rack servers sharing a storage array still have their own power, cooling and switch connections.

prompt: An administrator is choosing between 1U and 2U models of the same rack server for a storage-heavy application server. The application needs 12 front drive bays and three full-height PCIe cards. What is the most important reason to choose the 2U model?

options.text: The taller chassis offers more drive bays and full-height PCIe slots than the 1U chassis
The 2U chassis is required to use redundant power supplies on servers of the same family
The 2U chassis allows mixing RDIMM and UDIMM memory that the 1U board does not support
The 2U chassis uses less power per server, so the rack's PDU can host more of them

explanation: A 2U chassis is twice the height of a 1U chassis, which leaves room for more front drive bays and full-height expansion cards. Chassis height has no effect on whether memory types can be mixed, and they never can. Many 1U servers have redundant power supplies. A larger chassis with more drives and cards normally draws more power, not less.

prompt: A file server holds 6 TB of data today. Data has grown by 25 percent each year, and that rate is expected to continue. Ignoring RAID overhead and free-space headroom, about how much capacity will the data need in three years?

options.text: About 11.7 TB
About 7.5 TB
About 18 TB
About 10.5 TB

explanation: Growth of 25 percent per year compounds, so 6 TB x 1.25 x 1.25 x 1.25 is about 11.7 TB. About 10.5 TB comes from adding 25 percent of the original 6 TB each year, which ignores compounding. About 7.5 TB is only one year of growth. About 18 TB assumes the data triples, which is far more than 25 percent per year.

prompt: A company is adding a new database server to an existing Fibre Channel SAN. The storage team will present LUNs to the server after the fabric switches are zoned. What must the administrator install in the server, and what identifier will the storage team need?

options.text: A Fibre Channel HBA, and its World Wide Port Names (WWPNs) for zoning and LUN masking
A RAID controller, and its serial number for zoning and LUN masking
An iSCSI-capable Ethernet NIC, and its iSCSI Qualified Name (IQN) for zoning and LUN masking
A SAS HBA with external ports, and the MAC addresses of its ports for zoning and LUN masking

explanation: Connecting to a Fibre Channel SAN requires a Fibre Channel host bus adapter, and FC zoning and LUN masking are configured using the HBA's World Wide Port Names. An iSCSI NIC and IQN are used for iSCSI, which runs over Ethernet rather than an FC fabric. SAS HBAs connect to direct-attached shelves and have no MAC addresses for a fabric. A RAID controller manages local disks and its serial number is not used in a SAN.

prompt: A new server is configured as an iSCSI initiator. The administrator can ping the storage array's target portal address from the server, but target discovery times out. A firewall between the server and the array only permits ICMP and TCP 443. What should the administrator ask the network team to allow?

options.text: TCP port 2049 from the server to the target portal
UDP port 3260 from the server to the target portal
TCP port 3260 from the server to the target portal
TCP port 445 from the server to the target portal

explanation: iSCSI runs over TCP, and its well-known port for target portals is 3260, so the firewall must allow TCP 3260. iSCSI does not use UDP, so opening UDP 3260 would not help. TCP 445 is used by SMB file sharing. TCP 2049 is the NFS port, used for file-level NAS access rather than iSCSI block storage.

prompt: An administrator is filling an empty 42U rack with two 2U UPS units, one 4U storage shelf, ten 1U servers, two 1U switches and one 1U patch panel. How much rack space will remain unused?

options.text: 17U, which is about 29.75 inches of vertical space
21U, which is about 52.5 inches of vertical space
21U, which is about 36.75 inches of vertical space
25U, which is about 43.75 inches of vertical space

explanation: The equipment uses 4U + 4U + 10U + 2U + 1U = 21U, leaving 21U of a 42U rack, and one rack unit is 1.75 inches, so 21U is about 36.75 inches. The 52.5-inch figure wrongly assumes 2.5 inches per unit. 17U results from counting each UPS as 4U, and 25U results from leaving the 4U storage shelf out of the total.

prompt: A storage array has two controllers in an active-passive arrangement: each LUN is owned by one controller, and the other takes over only if the owner fails. What must be configured on each server attached to the array so that it keeps access to its LUNs when a controller fails?

options.text: A RAID 1 mirror inside the server, so the LUN is copied to local disks on controller failure
NIC teaming on the server's management interfaces, so the controllers see a single address
A second HBA connected to the same controller port, so the host has two cables to one path
Multipath I/O with paths to both controllers, so the host can switch to the surviving path

explanation: With active-passive controllers, a host needs paths to both controllers and multipath software so it can use the passive controller's path when the owner fails. Teaming management NICs has nothing to do with storage paths. A local RAID 1 mirror does not replicate a SAN LUN. Two HBAs cabled to the same controller still fail together when that controller fails.

prompt: An analytics cluster needs a storage tier with the lowest possible latency and highest IOPS for its scratch data. Cost per terabyte is secondary. Which media type should the administrator choose?

options.text: NVMe SSDs attached over PCIe
SATA SSDs on a RAID controller
10,000 RPM SAS hard disk drives
7,200 RPM nearline SAS drives

explanation: NVMe drives connect directly over PCIe and use a protocol designed for flash, giving the lowest latency and highest IOPS of these options. SATA SSDs are flash too but are limited by the SATA interface and AHCI command model. Any spinning hard drive, including 10,000 RPM SAS, has seek and rotational delay far higher than flash. Nearline drives are the slowest of the four and are chosen for low cost per terabyte.

prompt: A logging server will write several terabytes of data per day to a pair of 3.84 TB SSDs. Earlier deployments using read-optimised SSDs wore out in under two years. Which specification should the administrator compare when selecting replacement drives?

options.text: The sequential read throughput, such as megabytes per second for large blocks
The form factor, such as 2.5-inch versus 3.5-inch
The interface generation, such as SATA 3 Gb/s versus SATA 6 Gb/s connectors
The endurance rating, such as drive writes per day (DWPD)

explanation: SSD endurance is rated as drive writes per day or total bytes written, and a write-heavy workload needs drives with a high rating. Sequential read throughput says nothing about how many writes the flash cells survive. Interface speed affects transfer rate, not wear. Form factor affects fit in the drive bay, not endurance.

prompt: A server has redundant power supplies. During a maintenance event, one PDU in the rack was switched off and the server lost power completely. Both power supplies were working. What should the administrator change?

options.text: Replace both power supplies with higher-wattage units of the same model
Connect each power supply to a different PDU fed from a different circuit
Set the power supplies to balanced mode in firmware so both share load
Connect both power supplies to the same PDU using two different outlets

explanation: Redundant power supplies only protect the server when each one is fed from an independent PDU and circuit, so losing one feed leaves the other running. Higher wattage does not help when both supplies lose their source together. Two outlets on the same PDU still share that PDU as a single point of failure. Load-sharing settings change how the supplies split the load, not where their power comes from.

prompt: A hypervisor host has two 25 GbE ports in a team for VM traffic. Both ports are cabled to the same top-of-rack switch. When that switch was rebooted for a firmware upgrade, all VMs on the host lost network connectivity. What change removes this single point of failure?

options.text: Add a third port to the team and cable it to the same switch as the existing two ports
Replace the two 25 GbE ports with a single 100 GbE port connected to the same switch
Configure the switch ports as access ports rather than trunks so that failover is faster
Cable each team member to a different switch and configure the team to fail over between them

explanation: Spreading team members across two physical switches means the host keeps connectivity when one switch fails or reboots. A third port on the same switch still fails with that switch. A single 100 GbE port adds bandwidth but removes link redundancy entirely. Changing the port mode does nothing about both links ending on one switch, and access ports would also break the VLAN trunking a hypervisor usually needs.

prompt: A new hypervisor host will carry VMs on VLANs 10, 20 and 30 over a pair of uplinks to the top-of-rack switch. Each VM's virtual network adapter is assigned its VLAN ID on the host. How must the switch ports connected to the host be configured?

options.text: As access ports in VLAN 10, with VLANs 20 and 30 learned from the host's traffic
As access ports in VLAN 1, with each VM's VLAN set only inside the guest OS
As routed ports with an IP address from each VLAN
As 802.1Q trunk ports that carry VLANs 10, 20 and 30 as tagged traffic

explanation: When the host tags frames with VLAN IDs, the switch ports must be trunk ports that accept 802.1Q tagged traffic for each VLAN. An access port carries only one untagged VLAN, and switches do not learn VLAN membership from traffic. Leaving ports in VLAN 1 would place everything in the default VLAN. A routed port is a layer 3 interface and does not carry multiple VLANs to a host.

prompt: An administrator needs to connect a server's two SFP28 ports to a top-of-rack switch with SFP28 ports in the same rack, about 2 meters away. The goal is the lowest cost and power use for these links. Which cabling choice is the best fit?

options.text: Single-mode fiber with long-range optical transceivers
Cat 5e patch cables with RJ45 adapters
Passive direct attach copper (DAC) cables
Multimode fiber with OM1 cable and SR optics

explanation: Passive DAC cables have SFP28 ends built onto twinax copper, are inexpensive, draw almost no power and are designed for short in-rack runs. Long-range single-mode optics are costly and meant for kilometres, not two meters. Cat 5e with RJ45 cannot carry 25 Gb/s SFP28 traffic. Older OM1 multimode fiber has very short reach at 25 Gb/s, and optics cost more than DAC.

prompt: A server in a remote data center has hung with no network response from the OS. No staff are on site. The administrator must view the console and power cycle the server. Which capability should have been configured during deployment to allow this?

options.text: Wake-on-LAN on the server's onboard network adapter
An SSH daemon on the production operating system
Remote Desktop enabled for administrators on the server's primary network adapter
The baseboard management controller on a dedicated management network port

explanation: A baseboard management controller (such as iDRAC, iLO or an IPMI/Redfish BMC) runs independently of the OS and provides a remote console and power control, so it works even when the OS hangs. Remote Desktop and SSH both depend on the operating system that has stopped responding. Wake-on-LAN can only power on a system that is off; it cannot show the console or reset a hung server.

prompt: A new server will boot its operating system from a single 4 TB virtual disk presented by the RAID controller. The administrator wants to use the entire disk as the boot drive. Which firmware mode and partition style should be configured?

options.text: UEFI boot mode with an MBR-partitioned disk
Legacy BIOS boot mode with an MBR-partitioned disk
UEFI boot mode with a GPT-partitioned disk
Legacy BIOS boot mode with a GPT-partitioned disk

explanation: MBR can address only about 2 TiB, so a 4 TB boot disk needs GPT, and booting a server OS from GPT requires UEFI mode. Legacy BIOS with MBR would leave capacity beyond 2 TiB unusable. Mainstream server operating systems such as Windows Server do not boot from GPT in legacy BIOS mode. UEFI with MBR still has the same 2 TiB limit.

prompt: To meet a new security standard, an administrator changes a server's firmware from legacy BIOS mode to UEFI mode. The server was installed years ago on an MBR disk and now reports that no bootable device is found. Why?

options.text: UEFI mode requires a TPM to be enabled before it can read any partition from the boot device
UEFI mode clears the boot order, and the server must be re-imaged to restore the boot entries
UEFI mode disables the RAID controller's option ROM, so the controller no longer presents any disks
UEFI boot expects a GPT disk with an EFI system partition, which the MBR installation does not have

explanation: UEFI firmware loads a boot loader from an EFI system partition, normally on a GPT disk, so a legacy MBR installation without one is not bootable in pure UEFI mode. UEFI uses UEFI drivers instead of legacy option ROMs but still sees the controller's disks. A TPM is not required to read a boot partition. Boot entries can be recreated, and re-imaging is not what fixes a missing EFI partition.

prompt: A company is deploying identical servers that each draw about 650 W. Each server has two power supplies, one on circuit A and one on circuit B, and each circuit must be able to carry the full load of every server on it if the other circuit fails. The circuits are 120 V, 20 A, and continuous load is limited to 80 percent of the breaker rating. What is the largest number of these servers that can share one pair of circuits?
explanation: Each server draws about 650 W / 120 V = 5.4 A, and one circuit may carry 80 percent of 20 A, which is 16 A, so it can safely carry two servers (10.8 A) but not three (16.3 A). Three servers exceed the 16 A continuous limit when one circuit carries everything. Four assumes the load is always split between the circuits, which fails when one circuit drops. Six ignores both the 80 percent rule and the failover requirement.

prompt: An administrator is planning a new rack layout that includes two rack-mount UPS units with internal batteries, a storage shelf full of drives, several 1U servers and two network switches. Where should the UPS units be mounted?

options.text: In the middle of the rack, between the servers and the storage shelf
Anywhere in the rack, because rack rails are rated for the full load
At the bottom of the rack, because they are the heaviest equipment
At the top of the rack, close to the switches and patch panels

explanation: Heavy equipment such as battery-filled UPS units belongs at the bottom of the rack to keep the centre of gravity low and reduce tipping risk. Mounting them at the top makes the rack top-heavy and dangerous to service. The middle still raises the centre of gravity compared with the bottom. Rail weight ratings do not remove the tipping risk of poor weight distribution.

prompt: A company wants to replace its separate rack servers, SAN array and storage switches with a platform where each node contributes CPU, memory and local drives to a software-defined storage pool, and capacity grows by adding identical nodes. Which approach meets this goal?

options.text: Direct-attached storage on each standalone server
Hyperconverged infrastructure
Converged infrastructure with a dedicated SAN
Blade servers with an external storage array

explanation: Hyperconverged infrastructure combines compute and storage in each node and pools the local drives with software-defined storage, so the cluster scales by adding nodes. Converged infrastructure packages servers, storage and networking together but still uses a separate storage array. Blade servers with an external array keep storage separate. Direct-attached storage on standalone servers is not pooled or shared.

prompt: A company runs a four-node hyperconverged cluster. Storage use is at 85 percent, but CPU and memory use are below 30 percent. The vendor only sells nodes with matching compute and storage. What is the main drawback of expanding the cluster in this situation?

options.text: Adding nodes for storage also buys compute and memory the cluster does not need
Adding nodes requires the cluster to be rebuilt and all VMs restored from backup
Adding nodes requires an external SAN to hold the storage metadata for the cluster
Adding nodes reduces storage resilience because data is spread across more drives

explanation: Hyperconverged clusters typically scale compute and storage together, so a storage-only need still means paying for unneeded CPU and memory. Hyperconverged platforms are designed to add nodes online without rebuilding the cluster. Spreading data across more nodes does not reduce resilience; the replication or erasure-coding policy sets that. Hyperconverged clusters keep metadata on the nodes and do not need an external SAN.

prompt: A retail chain wants each store to keep processing card-present transactions and inventory lookups with low latency even when the store's WAN link to the central data center is down. Which approach fits this requirement?

options.text: Move all store workloads to a public cloud region and add a second internet circuit at each store
Run the store workloads on a central cluster and give each store thin clients over a VPN tunnel
Increase the WAN bandwidth to each store so that transactions finish faster at the data center
Deploy small edge servers in each store that run the workloads locally and sync with the data center

explanation: Edge computing places compute close to where data is created, so the store keeps working locally and synchronises when the WAN returns. Moving everything to a public cloud still depends on the store's connectivity. Thin clients over a VPN stop working when the link drops. More bandwidth does not help when the link is down, and it does not remove round-trip latency.

prompt: A factory has thousands of sensors that each send readings many times per second. Sending all raw data to the cloud would cost too much in bandwidth. Which edge design best addresses this?

options.text: Send the raw readings to the cloud over a VPN so that the provider does not charge for the traffic
Process and filter the readings on local edge servers and forward only summaries and anomalies to the cloud
Buffer the raw readings on each sensor and upload all of them to the cloud overnight in one batch
Compress the raw readings with a lossless algorithm and stream every reading to the cloud in real time

explanation: Edge servers can aggregate, filter and analyse data near the source, sending only what the central systems need, which greatly cuts bandwidth. Uploading everything overnight still moves all the raw data and delays results. Lossless compression reduces the size but still sends every reading. Using a VPN does not change how much data crosses the link or how egress and bandwidth are billed.

prompt: A company is placing edge servers in unattended telecom cabinets at remote sites. Which consideration is the most specific to this edge deployment compared with servers in the main data center?

options.text: A hypervisor certified on the main data center's hardware compatibility list
Full-disk encryption, tamper-resistant enclosures and remote out-of-band management
Blade servers so that they share power and cooling with the cabinet
A dedicated SAN connection so their data is stored in the main data center

explanation: Edge equipment often sits in places with little physical security and no staff, so encrypting data, resisting tampering and managing the hardware remotely are key concerns. A SAN connection back to the main site defeats local processing and is rarely practical. The HCL matters for any hypervisor but is not specific to edge sites. Blade chassis need data center power and cooling and are a poor fit for small cabinets.

prompt: An operations team wants every new test environment to be created from text files kept in version control, so that environments are identical, reviewed through pull requests and recreated on demand. Which practice should the team adopt?

options.text: Golden VM snapshots
Infrastructure as code
Thin provisioning
Manual runbooks

explanation: Infrastructure as code defines servers, networks and storage in machine-readable files that can be versioned, reviewed and applied repeatedly to produce the same result. Manual runbooks rely on people following steps and drift between runs. A golden snapshot copies one VM but does not define networks or other resources and is not reviewable as code. Thin provisioning is a storage allocation method, not a way to define environments.

prompt: An administrator applies the same infrastructure as code definition three times in a row. The first run creates two VMs and a firewall rule; the second and third runs report no changes. Which property of the tool does this demonstrate?

options.text: Elasticity
Orchestration
Idempotency
Immutability

explanation: An idempotent tool compares the desired state with the current state and changes only what differs, so applying the same definition again makes no further changes. Elasticity is the ability to add or remove capacity with demand. Immutability means replacing resources instead of changing them in place. Orchestration coordinates multi-step workflows across systems; it does not describe repeat runs making no changes.

prompt: A team manages its servers with infrastructure as code. During an outage, a technician changed a load balancer setting by hand in the management portal. What problem does this create, and how should the team resolve it?

options.text: The code is now locked by the portal; delete the code repository and rebuild it from the portal's settings
The portal change is permanent; future runs will skip that load balancer until it is manually re-created
The code becomes invalid; convert the infrastructure back to manual management until the next release
The live setting has drifted; commit the change to code through review or reapply the code

explanation: A manual change creates configuration drift, where the real environment no longer matches the code, and the next run may overwrite it. The fix is to bring code and reality back together, either by committing the change or reapplying the definition. Portals do not lock code repositories. IaC tools do not skip resources because of manual edits; they detect the difference. Abandoning IaC throws away its benefits over one change.

prompt: A company's network team wants to define VLANs, routing and firewall policy centrally in software and push them to switches through a controller, rather than configuring each switch by hand. Which concept does this describe?

options.text: Spanning tree, where switches elect a root bridge and block redundant paths to prevent loops
Software-defined networking, where a controller separates the control plane from the data plane
Link aggregation, where several switch ports are bonded to carry traffic as one logical link
Network address translation, where private addresses are mapped to public addresses at the edge

explanation: Software-defined networking moves the control logic into a central controller that programs the forwarding devices, so policy is defined once in software. Link aggregation combines physical links for bandwidth and redundancy but is configured per device. NAT translates addresses and does not centralise configuration. Spanning tree prevents loops and is a per-switch protocol, not a central control model.

prompt: A company is consolidating 40 physical application servers onto three new hosts in its data center. It needs the best performance and the smallest attack surface for the virtualization layer. Which hypervisor type should it use?

options.text: A Type 2 hypervisor installed on a full desktop OS on each host
A Type 1 hypervisor installed directly on the server hardware
A Type 2 hypervisor installed on a minimal server OS on each host
A container runtime installed on a general-purpose OS on each host

explanation: A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, which gives better performance and a smaller attack surface than running on a general-purpose OS. Any Type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on a host OS, so it adds that OS's overhead and vulnerabilities even when the OS is minimal. A container runtime shares the host kernel and cannot run the full VMs that consolidating different physical servers usually requires.

prompt: A developer needs to run three small test VMs with different operating systems on a laptop that must keep running its normal desktop applications. Which virtualization option is the best fit?

options.text: A hyperconverged cluster built from the laptop and two spare desktop machines
A Type 1 hypervisor installed in place of the laptop's existing operating system
A container runtime with one container for each of the three operating systems
A Type 2 hypervisor running as an application on the laptop's operating system

explanation: A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs on top of an existing OS, so the laptop keeps its desktop applications while hosting the test VMs. Installing a Type 1 hypervisor would replace the laptop's normal OS. A hyperconverged cluster is a production data center platform, not a developer setup. Containers share the host's kernel, so they cannot run different operating systems such as Windows and Linux side by side the way VMs can.

prompt: A web team needs to run 50 copies of a stateless API service, start new copies in seconds when traffic rises, and package each copy with its exact library versions. Which technology best fits?

options.text: Full VMs cloned from a template
Containers built from a single image
Type 2 hypervisors on each developer workstation
Physical servers in an active-passive cluster

explanation: Containers share the host kernel and package an application with its dependencies, so they start in seconds and many can run densely from one image. Full VMs each boot their own OS, which is slower and uses more resources per copy. Physical servers in an active-passive cluster cannot scale out in seconds. Type 2 hypervisors on workstations are for local testing, not production scaling.

prompt: A vendor application must run on a kernel version and kernel modules that differ from the host OS used by the company's container platform. Why is a VM a better choice than a container for this application?

options.text: Containers cannot be given network addresses, while a VM has a virtual NIC with its own address
Containers share the host's kernel, while a VM runs its own kernel and can load its own modules
Containers cannot store application files, while a VM has a virtual disk for its program files
Containers cannot be limited in CPU or memory, while a VM's resources can be reserved or capped

explanation: Every container on a host uses the host OS kernel, so an application that needs a different kernel or its own kernel modules needs a VM with its own guest OS. Containers do include application files in their image layers and can use volumes. Containers can be given network addresses through the container networking stack. Container runtimes can limit CPU and memory through control groups.

prompt: An administrator must ensure that NTP servers, SSH settings and a list of approved packages stay the same on 300 Linux servers, and that any server that drifts is reported and corrected automatically. Which approach should be used?

options.text: A monitoring dashboard that graphs CPU, memory and disk use for each server
A configuration management tool enforcing a desired state on every server
A backup schedule that takes a nightly image-level backup of each server
A ticketing system that assigns a monthly review task for each server

explanation: Configuration management tools such as Ansible, Puppet or Chef define the desired settings once, apply them to every server and detect and correct drift. A monitoring dashboard shows performance but does not enforce settings. Nightly image backups protect data but would restore drifted settings as easily as good ones. A monthly ticket depends on manual work and leaves servers out of compliance between reviews.

prompt: During an outage review, a team could not quickly tell which applications depended on a failed database cluster. Which configuration management practice would have given them this information?

options.text: A vulnerability scan report that lists open ports and missing patches on each server
A configuration management database recording items and their relationships
A software bill of materials that lists every library included in each application
A network diagram that shows the physical cabling between racks and core switches

explanation: A configuration management database (CMDB) tracks configuration items such as servers, databases and applications along with the dependencies between them, which is what the team needed. A vulnerability scan lists security weaknesses, not service dependencies. An SBOM lists software components inside an application, not which applications use a database. A cabling diagram shows physical connections, not application dependencies.

prompt: An online retailer's traffic triples for six weeks each holiday season. Buying enough on-premises servers for the peak would leave them idle for most of the year. Which cloud model best addresses this?

options.text: Private cloud built on additional servers purchased for the peak season
Community cloud shared with other retailers that have the same peak season
Private cloud hosted by a colocation provider on leased dedicated servers
Public cloud with pay-as-you-go resources added for the peak season

explanation: Public cloud lets the retailer add capacity on demand for the peak and pay only while using it. A private cloud on purchased servers is still sized for the peak and sits idle the rest of the year. A community cloud shared with retailers that peak at the same time would be stretched at the same moment. Leased dedicated servers in colocation are still fixed capacity that the retailer pays for all year.

prompt: A government contractor must keep a classified workload on infrastructure dedicated to its own organisation, under its own control, while still giving internal teams self-service provisioning of VMs. Which cloud model fits?

options.text: Public cloud
Private cloud
Community cloud
Multitenant SaaS

explanation: A private cloud is built for a single organisation, which keeps the workload on dedicated infrastructure while still offering cloud features such as self-service provisioning. Public cloud runs on shared provider infrastructure. Multitenant SaaS delivers a finished application to many customers and does not provide VM provisioning. A community cloud is shared by several organisations, so it is not dedicated to one.

prompt: A company keeps its customer database on servers in its own data center for regulatory reasons, but runs its web front end in a public cloud so it can scale. The two are connected by a site-to-site VPN. Which cloud model is this?

options.text: Hybrid cloud
Edge computing
Public cloud
Private cloud

explanation: A hybrid cloud combines on-premises or private infrastructure with public cloud resources that work together, as the database and web tier do here. A private cloud alone would not include the public cloud front end. A public cloud alone would not include the on-premises database. Edge computing places compute near users or devices, which is not what this design describes.

prompt: A company wants to stop running its own mail servers. The provider must handle the application, OS patching, servers and storage, while the company only manages users and mailbox settings. Which service model fits?

options.text: Software as a service (SaaS)
Colocation hosting
Platform as a service (PaaS)
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)

explanation: With SaaS the provider runs the complete application and all layers beneath it, and the customer only configures and uses it. With IaaS the customer still installs and patches the OS and mail software. PaaS gives developers a managed runtime to deploy their own code, not a finished mail service. Colocation only provides rack space, power and cooling for the customer's own hardware.

prompt: A development team wants to deploy its web application code without installing, patching or scaling the operating system and web server beneath it. Which cloud service model meets this need?

options.text: Platform as a service (PaaS)
Software as a service (SaaS)
Bare-metal hosting
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)

explanation: PaaS provides a managed runtime where developers deploy their own code while the provider manages the OS, middleware and scaling. IaaS gives VMs that the customer must patch and configure. SaaS delivers a finished application rather than a place to run custom code. Bare-metal hosting gives whole physical servers that the customer must build and maintain.

prompt: A company migrates its application servers to VMs in a public cloud IaaS offering. A critical OS vulnerability is announced for the guest operating system. Who is responsible for patching it?

options.text: The cloud provider, because IaaS includes managed OS patching
Neither party, because cloud VMs are patched by the hypervisor
The company, because the customer manages the guest OS in IaaS
The cloud provider, because the provider owns the physical hosts

explanation: Under the IaaS shared responsibility model, the provider secures the physical facility, hardware and hypervisor, while the customer installs, configures and patches the guest OS and applications. Owning the physical hosts does not make the provider responsible for the customer's OS. Standard IaaS does not include OS patching; that is a feature of PaaS or managed services. A hypervisor does not patch guest operating systems.

prompt: Which two statements correctly compare the cloud service models? (Choose two.)

options.text: In SaaS, the customer installs the application on VMs provided by the vendor
In PaaS, the customer manages the operating system patches on the platform's servers
In IaaS, the customer manages the operating system and the applications installed on it
In IaaS, the provider manages the guest operating system and the customer's data
In SaaS, the provider manages the application as well as the infrastructure under it

explanation: In IaaS the provider supplies compute, storage and networking while the customer manages the OS and everything above it, and in SaaS the provider runs the whole application stack. In PaaS the provider, not the customer, manages the OS beneath the runtime. SaaS customers do not install the application at all. IaaS providers do not manage the guest OS, and the customer is always responsible for its own data.

prompt: An administrator builds a new file server VM for 300 users using exactly the minimum CPU, RAM and disk listed in the OS vendor's system requirements. The installation succeeds, but users report very slow file access once the server is in production. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Minimum requirements assume Server Core; any GUI install needs four times the listed figures
Minimums only ensure the OS installs and runs; size the VM for the actual workload
Minimum requirements include file-sharing load; slow access must be caused by the client network
Minimums apply only to physical servers; VMs need double the figures

explanation: Vendor minimums describe the smallest configuration on which the OS will install and boot, and they do not account for roles, applications or user load, so production sizing must be based on the workload. There is no rule that VMs need exactly double or that a GUI needs four times the figures. Minimums never include application load, so blaming the client network ignores the undersized server.

prompt: An administrator tries to install a current server OS release on a repurposed older server. The installer stops early, stating that the processor is not supported, even though the server has enough RAM and disk space. What should the administrator check?

options.text: Whether the firmware clock is set after the OS release date
Whether the CPU has the instruction set features the OS vendor requires
Whether the server has enough free PCIe slots for the OS vendor's required expansion cards
Whether the boot disk is formatted with the filesystem the OS will use after installation

explanation: Modern server operating systems list required CPU capabilities, such as a 64-bit instruction set and specific extensions, and the installer refuses processors that lack them. PCIe slot count is not part of OS processor requirements. The installer formats the target disk itself, so the existing filesystem does not matter. The firmware clock date does not affect processor support checks.

prompt: A Linux server has Secure Boot enabled. After the administrator installs a custom-compiled kernel module for a storage adapter, loading the module fails with "Key was rejected by service". What should the administrator do to keep Secure Boot enabled and load the module?

options.text: Switch the firmware to legacy BIOS mode so Secure Boot checks only the boot loader file
Rebuild the initramfs without the module so the kernel loads it later without a signature
Sign the module with a key and enroll that key as a Machine Owner Key so the boot chain trusts it
Disable the TPM in firmware so the kernel stops checking module signatures during boot

explanation: With Secure Boot, the kernel only loads modules signed with a trusted key, so the fix is to sign the module and enroll the signing key (for example with mokutil) so shim and the kernel accept it. The TPM is separate from Secure Boot signature enforcement. Loading the module later from disk still requires a valid signature. Legacy BIOS mode turns Secure Boot off entirely, which the administrator wants to avoid.

prompt: An administrator wants to enable Secure Boot on a server, but the option is unavailable in the firmware setup. The server's firmware is configured with the compatibility support module (CSM) enabled for legacy boot. What must be changed first?

options.text: Clear the RAID configuration, because Secure Boot cannot start from a RAID volume
Reset the BMC to factory defaults, because Secure Boot is controlled by the BMC
Switch to UEFI boot mode with CSM disabled; Secure Boot needs native UEFI
Install a TPM 2.0 module, because Secure Boot is only offered when a TPM is present

explanation: Secure Boot is a UEFI feature that validates signed boot components, so it is only available when the system boots in native UEFI mode without legacy compatibility. Secure Boot does not need a TPM, although the two are often used together. The BMC is not what enables Secure Boot in the platform firmware. Secure Boot works with boot volumes presented by supported RAID controllers.

prompt: A technician is on site at a branch office to reinstall a server's operating system. The server has no optical drive, and the technician has a laptop and the vendor's installation ISO. Which installation media should the technician prepare?

options.text: A DVD burned from the ISO image
An SD card containing the ISO file
A network share containing the ISO file
A bootable USB flash drive created from the ISO image

explanation: Writing the ISO to a USB flash drive makes it bootable, and servers can boot from USB without an optical drive. A DVD needs an optical drive, which the server does not have. Copying the ISO file onto an SD card does not make the card bootable. A network share holding the ISO cannot be booted directly; booting over the network needs a PXE or similar service.

prompt: A hypervisor vendor has warned that booting hosts solely from SD cards leads to card failures because of frequent writes. A host boots from a mirrored pair of SD cards and the cards keep failing. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Enable write caching on the SD card reader so writes are held in memory before reaching the cards
Replace the mirrored SD cards with a single USB flash drive
Replace the SD cards with larger SD cards of the same type so the writes spread over more space
Move boot and system data to durable media, such as an SSD or M.2 boot module

explanation: SD cards and USB flash drives have low write endurance, so hosts that write logs and system data to them wear the cards out; moving that data to durable SSD or M.2 boot media addresses the cause. Larger SD cards have the same weak endurance. Write caching delays the writes but still sends them to the cards and risks data loss on power failure. A single USB flash drive has similar endurance and also removes the mirror.

prompt: A Linux server will not boot after a failed update, and the administrator needs to copy configuration files from its disks before attempting repairs, without changing the installed OS. Which installation media option is most useful?

options.text: Boot the server from live media and mount the server's disks from the live environment
Boot from a PXE server and select an unattended installation profile to rebuild the server
Run an in-place upgrade from the installation ISO so the installer repairs the broken files
Run a clean installation over the existing OS and then copy the files from the new install

explanation: Live media runs a complete OS from the USB or DVD without installing it, so the administrator can mount the server's disks and copy files without modifying the installation. A clean install overwrites the disk and destroys the files to be saved. An in-place upgrade changes the installed OS before the files are safe. An unattended PXE installation rebuilds the server and would erase its data.

prompt: An administrator downloads a server OS ISO image from the vendor's website. Before using it to install production servers, the administrator wants to confirm the file was not corrupted or altered. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Compute the ISO's SHA-256 hash and compare it with the vendor's published value
Scan the ISO with antivirus software and confirm that no threats are found
Check that the ISO's file size is close to the size listed on the download page
Mount the ISO and confirm the file count matches the vendor's release notes

explanation: A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 changes if even one bit of the file changes, so matching the vendor's published value confirms integrity. A file count can match even when file contents are damaged or altered. File size can be the same after corruption or tampering. Antivirus scanning detects known malware but cannot prove the image is unaltered.

prompt: A company must deploy the same server OS build to 40 new servers with identical disk layout, regional settings and administrator credentials, and no technician should have to answer installer prompts. Which installation approach meets this requirement?

options.text: An unattended installation that reads its settings from an answer file
A live media session on each server's local console
An in-place upgrade from the previous OS version
An attended installation that follows a detailed written checklist for each server

explanation: An unattended installation uses an answer file, such as unattend.xml for Windows or a kickstart file for RHEL-based Linux, to supply every installer setting so no prompts appear and each build is the same. An attended install with a checklist still needs a person at each prompt and allows mistakes. An in-place upgrade requires an existing OS on new servers that have none. Live media runs an OS temporarily and does not install it.

prompt: An administrator boots the RHEL installer over the network and adds inst.ks=http://deploy.example.com/web01.cfg to the boot options. What does this option do?

options.text: It points the installer to a kickstart file that answers the installation settings automatically
It points the installer to a disk image that is written to the server's disk block by block
It points the installer to a local mirror that holds the package repository for installation
It points the installer to a web console where an administrator answers the prompts remotely

explanation: The inst.ks boot option tells the RHEL installer where to find a kickstart file, which holds the answers for an automated installation. The installation package source is set with a different option, inst.repo. Kickstart drives the normal installer rather than writing a raw disk image. Kickstart removes the need for prompts instead of sending them to a web console.

prompt: A server that hosted a decommissioned application will be repurposed as a database server. Its old OS has years of leftover software, accounts and configuration changes. The security team wants nothing from the old build to carry over. Which installation type should the administrator use?

options.text: A clean installation that repartitions the disks and installs a fresh OS
A minor version update of the existing OS
A repair installation over the existing OS
An in-place upgrade to the latest OS release, which replaces system files but keeps settings

explanation: A clean installation wipes the existing system and installs a new OS, so no old software, accounts or settings remain. An in-place upgrade is designed to keep applications, settings and data. A repair installation also keeps the existing configuration. A minor version update only patches the current OS and keeps everything on it.

prompt: A company wants to move a file server from the previous major OS release to the current one while keeping its installed roles, shares, settings and data, and without rebuilding the server. What should the administrator confirm before starting?

options.text: That a clean installation media set is available, and that the data volumes have been reformatted beforehand
That the disks are converted to dynamic disks first
That the server can PXE boot, and that the deployment server has an image for the new OS release
That the in-place upgrade path is supported, and that a verified backup exists

explanation: An in-place upgrade keeps roles, settings and data, but vendors only support specific upgrade paths between versions, and a backup is essential in case the upgrade fails. A clean installation and reformatting would discard the data and settings the company wants to keep. PXE imaging replaces the OS rather than upgrading it. Converting to dynamic disks is not an upgrade prerequisite, and Microsoft has deprecated dynamic disks.

prompt: An administrator is building a Windows Server golden image that will be captured and deployed to many servers with an imaging tool. What must be done before capturing the image?

options.text: Run Sysprep with the generalize option to remove computer-specific information
Assign a static IP address so deployed servers keep a known network setting
Join the reference server to the domain so the image is already a domain member
Enable BitLocker on the reference server so each deployed copy is encrypted

explanation: Sysprep /generalize removes machine-specific data such as the computer name and security identifiers so each deployed copy is set up as a unique machine. Joining the reference machine to the domain would leave every copy with the same domain identity, which causes conflicts. BitLocker on the reference image does not carry over in a usable way and should be enabled after deployment. A static IP in the image would cause address conflicts across all deployed servers.

prompt: A virtualization team deploys about ten new Linux VMs each week. Each must start from the same hardened build and then receive a unique hostname and IP address. Which deployment method should the team use?

options.text: Clone each VM from a VM template and apply a guest customization profile for its name and address
Take a snapshot of one VM and revert it each time a new VM is needed for the team
Install each VM from the vendor ISO by hand and apply the hardening checklist afterwards
Copy a running production VM's virtual disk and boot the copy with its original settings

explanation: Template-based deployment clones a prepared, hardened VM, and a customization profile assigns each clone its own identity, such as hostname and IP address. Copying a running production VM's disk duplicates its identity and may copy inconsistent data. Manual ISO installs are slow and drift from the standard. Reverting a snapshot changes the same VM back rather than creating new ones.

prompt: A team runs RHEL 9.4 on its application servers. Which change should be treated as a major version change that needs a full compatibility test plan rather than the normal monthly patch process?

options.text: Applying the latest security errata for RHEL 9.4
Moving the servers from RHEL 9.4 to RHEL 9.6
Updating the kernel package within RHEL 9.4
Moving the servers from RHEL 9.4 to RHEL 10

explanation: A change in the first number (9 to 10) is a major version, which can remove or change features, packages and defaults and so needs full testing. A move from 9.4 to 9.6 is a minor version update within the same major release, designed to stay compatible. Security errata and kernel updates within 9.4 are routine updates handled by normal patching.

prompt: An administrator must install an OS on a new server in a colocation facility 800 km away. The server is racked, powered and cabled, including its dedicated management port, but nobody is available on site. How can the administrator perform the installation?

options.text: Use Remote Desktop to the server's primary NIC and start the installer from the desktop
Use SSH to the server's primary NIC and copy the ISO to the boot disk before rebooting
Use the BMC's remote console and virtual media to mount the ISO and run the installer remotely
Ship a bootable USB drive to the facility and ask the provider to leave it in the server

explanation: Out-of-band management through the BMC (for example iDRAC, iLO or a Redfish-capable controller) provides a remote console and virtual media, so the administrator can boot the ISO and complete the installation without any OS on the server. Shipping a USB drive still needs someone on site to handle it and would delay the work. Remote Desktop and SSH both need a running OS, which a new server does not have.

prompt: A security team wants new Windows Server installations to have the smallest attack surface and fewer updates to install, and the servers will be managed remotely with PowerShell and Windows Admin Center. Which installation option should the administrator choose?

options.text: Nano Server
Windows client with RSAT
Server with Desktop Experience
Server Core

explanation: Server Core omits the desktop shell and many graphical components, which reduces the attack surface and the number of patches, and it is designed for remote management. Desktop Experience installs the full GUI, which adds components to patch. Nano Server is now offered only as a container base image, not as a host installation option. A Windows client with RSAT is a management workstation, not a server installation.

prompt: A new server will host a Type 1 hypervisor. There is no OS on the server, and the hypervisor will be installed directly onto the server's boot drive. What kind of installation is this?

options.text: A nested virtualization install
An in-place upgrade
A bare-metal installation
A template-based deployment

explanation: A bare-metal installation puts the OS or hypervisor directly on physical hardware that has no existing OS. An in-place upgrade needs an existing OS to upgrade. Nested virtualization runs a hypervisor inside a VM, which is the opposite of this setup. Template-based deployment clones VMs from a template, which needs a hypervisor that does not exist yet.

prompt: A PXE deployment server has been imaging older servers that use legacy BIOS boot without any problem. New servers configured for UEFI boot obtain an IP address but then fail to start the network boot program. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: DHCP gives all clients the BIOS boot file instead of a UEFI boot file
The UEFI servers must be joined to the domain before they are allowed to download boot files
The DHCP scope has no free addresses left for the UEFI servers
The TFTP server only accepts connections from servers whose MAC address it has seen before

explanation: UEFI and BIOS clients need different network boot programs, so DHCP must return a UEFI boot file to UEFI clients, typically by checking the client architecture option. The servers did receive IP addresses, so the scope is not exhausted. TFTP servers do not normally restrict by previously seen MAC addresses. A machine cannot join a domain before it has an OS, so that is not a requirement for PXE.

prompt: During PXE deployments, new servers receive an IP address and the name of the boot file from DHCP, but then show a timeout while downloading the boot file. A firewall was recently placed between the server VLAN and the deployment server. What should the administrator check?

options.text: That the firewall permits HTTPS on TCP port 443 from the servers to the internet proxy
That the firewall permits SMB on TCP port 445 from the servers to the deployment server
That the firewall permits TFTP on UDP port 69 from the servers to the deployment server
That the firewall permits DHCP on UDP ports 67 and 68 between the servers and the router

explanation: Classic PXE downloads the boot file with TFTP, which starts on UDP port 69, so a new firewall that blocks it causes a timeout after DHCP succeeds. DHCP is already working because the servers received addresses and boot file names. SMB is not used for the initial PXE boot file download. Internet HTTPS access is unrelated to fetching the boot file from the deployment server.

prompt: A company ships new servers directly from the manufacturer to 25 branch offices that have no IT staff. When a server is cabled and powered on, it should contact the company's provisioning service, install its OS and apply its configuration with no on-site setup. Which deployment approach is this?

options.text: Zero-touch provisioning
In-place upgrading
Live media booting
Attended installation

explanation: Zero-touch provisioning lets a device configure itself from a central service when it first connects, with no technician involvement on site. An attended installation needs a person answering prompts. Live media runs an OS temporarily from removable media and needs someone to insert and boot it. An in-place upgrade updates an OS that is already installed.

prompt: A Linux storage server must protect against silent data corruption with end-to-end checksums, pool several disks without a separate volume manager and take near-instant snapshots. Which filesystem best fits these requirements?

options.text: NTFS
ext4
ZFS
VMFS

explanation: ZFS combines volume management and the filesystem, checksums all data and metadata to detect corruption (and repair it when redundancy exists) and uses copy-on-write for fast snapshots. ext4 checksums metadata but not file data, and it relies on LVM or another layer to pool disks. NTFS is a Windows filesystem without data checksums. VMFS is VMware's clustered filesystem for VM datastores, not a general Linux storage filesystem.

prompt: An administrator is installing Windows Server on a new host that will store Hyper-V VMs on a separate data volume. The administrator wants to use ReFS. Where can ReFS be used on this host?

options.text: On both the OS boot volume and the VM data volume
On the VM data volume, while the OS boot volume uses NTFS
On neither volume, because ReFS is only used by Linux
On the OS boot volume, while the VM data volume uses NTFS

explanation: Windows Server cannot boot from ReFS, so the OS volume uses NTFS, while ReFS is well suited to data volumes such as Hyper-V VM storage. Putting ReFS on the boot volume is not supported, which rules out the boot-volume and both-volumes choices. ReFS is a Microsoft filesystem, not a Linux one.

prompt: A newly installed server has a 3 TB data disk. The administrator initialised it as MBR during setup, and only about 2 TB can be allocated to partitions. What should the administrator do to use the full capacity?

options.text: Convert the disk to a dynamic disk and extend the volume
Format the partition with a larger allocation unit size
Create four primary partitions to cover the full disk
Convert the empty disk to GPT and create the partition again

explanation: MBR uses 32-bit sector addressing that limits it to about 2 TiB, while GPT supports far larger disks, so the empty disk should be converted to GPT. Dynamic disks on MBR are still bound by the MBR limit, and Microsoft has deprecated dynamic disks. Allocation unit size affects how space is used within a filesystem, not the partition table limit. More MBR partitions cannot address space beyond the 2 TiB limit.

prompt: During installation of a Linux server, the administrator expects /var to need more space within a year and wants to grow it later by adding a disk, without repartitioning or downtime. What should the administrator choose in the installer?

options.text: Create /var as a dynamic disk volume during installation
Create /var as a logical volume in an LVM volume group
Create /var as a fixed primary partition on the first disk
Create /var on a basic disk with an extended partition

explanation: With LVM, a new disk can be added to the volume group and the logical volume and its filesystem extended online, without repartitioning. A fixed primary partition can only grow into adjacent free space on the same disk. Dynamic disks are a Windows feature, not a Linux installer option. An extended partition is an MBR construct that does not let a filesystem span a newly added disk.

prompt:
An administrator extends a logical volume on a Linux server with the command below. The command succeeds, but df still shows the old size for the ext4 filesystem mounted at /data.

# lvextend -L +100G /dev/vg_data/lv_data
  Logical volume vg_data/lv_data successfully resized.

What should the administrator run next?

options.text: xfs_growfs /dev/vg_data/lv_data
resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_data
pvcreate /dev/vg_data/lv_data
mkfs.ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_data

explanation: lvextend grows the logical volume but not the filesystem inside it unless the -r option is used, so resize2fs is needed to grow ext4 into the new space, and it can do so while mounted. xfs_growfs is for XFS filesystems, not ext4. pvcreate initialises a disk or partition as an LVM physical volume and is not run against a logical volume. mkfs.ext4 would create a new empty filesystem and destroy the data.

prompt: A Linux server has several data disks. After a controller was replaced, the disk previously named /dev/sdc came up as /dev/sdd, and the server failed to mount /data at boot. How should the administrator configure /etc/fstab to prevent this?

options.text: Reference the filesystem by its mount point name instead of by its device name
Reference the filesystem by its UUID instead of by its /dev/sdX device name
Reference the filesystem by its controller port number instead of its device name
Reference the filesystem by its partition number instead of by its device name

explanation: Kernel device names such as /dev/sdc can change when hardware or detection order changes, while a filesystem UUID stays with the filesystem, so fstab entries using UUID= mount reliably. The mount point is the target, not a way to identify the source device. A partition number is still tied to a changing device name. fstab has no option to identify filesystems by controller port number.

prompt: A Windows file server administrator needs to combine free space from several new disks into one large, resilient volume. A colleague suggests converting the disks to dynamic disks and creating a spanned volume. What should the administrator do instead?

options.text: Use a dynamic spanned volume, because spanning adds parity across the disks
Use Storage Spaces on basic disks, because Microsoft has deprecated dynamic disks
Use one MBR basic disk per volume, because MBR supports spanning without limits
Use a dynamic striped volume, because striping tolerates the loss of one disk

explanation: Microsoft has deprecated dynamic disks and recommends Storage Spaces for pooling disks with resiliency. A spanned volume simply joins disks end to end with no parity, so losing any disk loses the volume. MBR basic disks cannot span disks and are limited to about 2 TiB each. A striped volume has no redundancy, so any single disk failure destroys it.

prompt: A new NTFS volume will hold SQL Server data and log files, which are read and written in large extents. The database vendor recommends a specific allocation unit size for these volumes. Which allocation unit size should the administrator choose when formatting?

options.text: 512 bytes
64 KB
2 MB
4 KB

explanation: Microsoft recommends a 64 KB NTFS allocation unit for SQL Server data and log volumes, which matches the size of a SQL Server extent and suits its I/O pattern. 4 KB is the general-purpose default and is not the recommendation for these volumes. 512 bytes is far smaller than needed and would increase metadata overhead. 2 MB is larger than recommended for this workload.

prompt:
A newly installed server cannot reach anything outside its own subnet. Its IP configuration is shown below.

IPv4 Address. . . . : 192.168.10.50
Subnet Mask . . . . : 255.255.255.0
Default Gateway . . : 192.168.1.1

What is the problem?

options.text: The default gateway is not on the server's subnet, so the server cannot reach it
The server is using an APIPA address because the DHCP server did not respond
The subnet mask must be 255.255.0.0 because every 192.168 address is a Class B network
The IP address is a public address that internet routers will refuse to forward

explanation: With a /24 mask the server's subnet is 192.168.10.0 to 192.168.10.255, and a default gateway must be an address on that subnet, so 192.168.1.1 cannot be reached. 192.168.0.0/16 is a private block that is normally divided into /24 or other subnets, so there is no rule that the mask must be 255.255.0.0. 192.168.10.50 is a private RFC 1918 address, not a public one. APIPA addresses come from 169.254.0.0/16, which this is not.

prompt: A server configured for DHCP shows the IPv4 address 169.254.33.17 with a 255.255.0.0 mask and cannot reach any other systems. What does this indicate?

options.text: The server received a lease from a DHCP server that is configured with the wrong scope
The server did not get a lease from a DHCP server and assigned itself an APIPA address
The server was assigned a static address from the reserved loopback address range
The server's NIC is connected to a VLAN that uses IPv6 only, so IPv4 was translated

explanation: Addresses in 169.254.0.0/16 are Automatic Private IP Addressing (link-local) addresses that a host assigns itself when it cannot reach a DHCP server. A DHCP server with a wrong scope would hand out an address from that scope, not 169.254.x.x. Loopback is 127.0.0.0/8. IPv6-only networks do not translate a host's IPv4 configuration into 169.254 addresses.

prompt: A server's NIC is configured in the OS to tag its traffic with VLAN ID 30. The switch port it connects to is configured as an access port in VLAN 20. What will happen?

options.text: The switch drops the tagged VLAN 30 frames, so the server has no connectivity
The server will negotiate the access port into a trunk that carries VLAN 30 traffic
The switch will create VLAN 30 automatically and forward the frames in that VLAN
The switch will remove the VLAN 30 tag and forward the frames normally in VLAN 20

explanation: An access port expects untagged frames for its configured VLAN, so tagged frames for a different VLAN are not forwarded and the server has no connectivity. The switch does not rewrite the tag into VLAN 20. Switches do not create VLANs automatically because they see tagged frames. A server OS does not negotiate a statically configured access port into a trunk.

prompt: A new application server must connect to a legacy reporting host named rpt01.corp.example.com, but the DNS team cannot create the record until next week. The application must work today on this one server only. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: A DNS suffix search list entry for corp.example.com on the server
A conditional forwarder for corp.example.com on the server's DNS client
A temporary entry for rpt01.corp.example.com in the server's hosts file
A DHCP reservation for rpt01.corp.example.com on the server's DHCP scope

explanation: The hosts file maps names to IP addresses locally and is checked before DNS, so an entry makes the name resolve on this one server until the DNS record exists, after which it should be removed. A suffix search list only appends domain names to short names and still needs a DNS record. Conditional forwarders are configured on DNS servers, not clients, and still need a server that has the record. A DHCP reservation assigns an address but does not create a name mapping for other hosts.

prompt: A company wants to give its internal servers IPv6 addresses that are routable inside the organisation but are never meant to be routed on the public internet. Which address range should the administrator use?

options.text: Unique local addresses from fd00::/8
Global unicast addresses from 2000::/3
Link-local addresses from fe80::/10
Multicast addresses from ff00::/8

explanation: Unique local addresses (fc00::/7, with fd00::/8 used for locally assigned prefixes) are routable within an organisation and are not routed on the internet, much like private IPv4 ranges. Link-local addresses work only on a single network segment and are not routed at all. Global unicast addresses are intended to be internet-routable. Multicast addresses identify groups, not individual servers.

prompt: A Linux web server will serve its site only over HTTPS and will be managed remotely with SSH. Which two inbound TCP ports should the administrator allow in the host firewall? (Choose two.)
explanation: SSH listens on TCP 22 and HTTPS on TCP 443, so those are the only ports this server needs open inbound. TCP 80 is plain HTTP, which the site does not serve. TCP 3389 is Remote Desktop Protocol, used for Windows remote management. TCP 23 is Telnet, an unencrypted protocol that should not be used for management.

prompt: A server's failed onboard NIC is replaced with a new adapter. The server is configured for DHCP and has a DHCP reservation so it always receives 10.20.5.15, but after the repair it receives a different address from the pool. What should the administrator update?

options.text: The DHCP reservation, so it uses the new adapter's MAC address
The server's hosts file, so it maps its own name to 10.20.5.15
The DHCP scope options, so the default gateway matches the new NIC
The DNS A record, so it points to the address from the pool

explanation: DHCP reservations are tied to a client's MAC address, and a replacement NIC has a new MAC, so the reservation must be updated to give the server its expected address again. Changing DNS to the pool address treats the symptom and the address may change later. Scope options such as the gateway are not linked to a specific NIC. A hosts file entry on the server itself does not change the address DHCP assigns.

prompt: An administrator installs a Type 1 hypervisor on a new server, but the installer reports that hardware virtualization support is not available. The server's processors support virtualization extensions. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: Disable the processors' extra cores in the firmware so the hypervisor can schedule them itself
Install additional DIMMs in every channel so the hypervisor reaches its minimum memory size
Enable memory mirroring in the firmware so the hypervisor has a protected copy of its memory
Enable the CPU virtualization extensions, such as Intel VT-x or AMD-V, in the server's firmware setup

explanation: Many servers ship with CPU virtualization extensions disabled, and hypervisors need them enabled in the BIOS/UEFI setup to run. Memory mirroring improves memory resilience but does not provide virtualization support. Disabling cores reduces capacity and does not enable virtualization. Adding memory addresses a memory shortage, not a missing CPU feature.

prompt: A company is deploying 802.1X authentication for its wireless network. The access points need a RADIUS server that checks users' Active Directory credentials and applies connection policies. Which Windows Server role should the administrator install?

options.text: DHCP Server
Network Policy Server (NPS)
Active Directory Certificate Services
Remote Access Server (RAS)

explanation: Network Policy Server is Microsoft's RADIUS server and proxy, which authenticates users against Active Directory and applies network policies for clients such as wireless access points. The Remote Access role provides VPN and routing services, and it can use NPS for authentication but is not itself the RADIUS server for access points. Certificate Services issues certificates, which 802.1X may use, but it does not authenticate RADIUS requests. DHCP hands out addresses and plays no part in authentication.

prompt: Remote employees need to connect from home to internal file shares through an encrypted tunnel that terminates on a Windows server at the company's network edge. Which server role provides this?

options.text: Web server providing HTTPS file downloads
Remote Desktop Session Host providing user sessions
Remote access server providing VPN connections
Network Policy Server providing RADIUS service

explanation: A remote access server (the Remote Access role with its VPN feature in Windows Server) terminates VPN tunnels and routes remote users onto the internal network so they can reach file shares. A Remote Desktop Session Host lets users run sessions on the server itself rather than connecting their device to the network. NPS can authenticate VPN users but does not terminate the tunnels. A web server publishing downloads does not give access to SMB file shares.

prompt: Forty office staff need to run a line-of-business application that only works on Windows. The company wants the application installed once on a central server, with each user running it in their own session from a thin client. Which server role should be deployed?

options.text: Network Policy Server
Print server
Remote Desktop Session Host
Remote access VPN server

explanation: A Remote Desktop Session Host (formerly Terminal Services) lets many users run applications in separate sessions on one server, which suits thin clients and central installation.
