options.text: A larger TCP receive window on the iSCSI initiator to absorb the outage
A second IP address on the same NIC used for the first iSCSI session
Multipath I/O (MPIO) with both iSCSI paths active or in failover
Jumbo frames on both NICs so each iSCSI session moves data faster

explanation: MPIO presents the two physical paths as one device and fails over when a path drops, so a switch outage does not take volumes offline. A second IP on the same NIC still uses the same physical path and switch. Jumbo frames and TCP window tuning affect throughput, not path failover.

prompt: A new MPLS circuit is down. The provider's technician tests up to the smart jack in the telecom room and reports that the circuit is clean. In this situation, what does the smart jack mark?

options.text: The point where the provider hands off to the customer's internal DHCP scope
The main distribution frame where all internal building cabling terminates
The demarcation point between the provider's responsibility and the customer's
The point where the customer's firewall begins filtering traffic from the internet

explanation: The demarc is where the provider's network ends and the customer's wiring and equipment begin, so a clean test to that point moves troubleshooting to the customer side. The firewall is customer equipment placed after the demarc. The MDF is the customer's main cabling hub, and DHCP is a logical service with no relation to the physical handoff.

prompt: A server vendor offers a backplane that supports tri-mode controllers, letting the same drive bays accept SAS, SATA or NVMe drives. Which drive interface standard was designed for this?

options.text: eSATA

explanation: U.3 was designed so one backplane and tri-mode controller can run SAS, SATA and NVMe drives in the same bays. U.2 supports NVMe drives in 2.5-inch bays but needs separate wiring from SAS/SATA. M.2 is a small card form factor usually used for boot drives, and eSATA is an external SATA connector.

prompt: A remote server will not boot after a kernel update and has no network connectivity. Its management controller supports several out-of-band methods. Which method lets the administrator watch the boot screen and interact with the bootloader menu remotely?

options.text: The controller's HTML5 remote console (virtual KVM)
SSH to the server's operating system
A Wake-on-LAN magic packet sent to the server's NIC
An SNMP query to the server's management controller

explanation: A remote console (virtual KVM) on the BMC shows the video output from power-on, so the administrator can see POST and choose a bootloader entry. SSH to the OS requires a running OS and network connectivity, which are missing. SNMP returns sensor and status data, and Wake-on-LAN only powers a system on.

prompt: An administrator finds that airflow through a rack is restricted and swapping a failed power supply took 20 minutes because of tangled cords. Which practice best addresses both problems?

options.text: Bundle all cables tightly across the rear exhaust area so they are kept in one place
Route labeled, right-length cables along the rack sides with management arms
Use the longest available cables everywhere so any device can reach any switch port
Remove the rack's rear doors so that cables can hang freely outside the rack frame

explanation: Routing labeled, correctly sized cables along the sides with management arms keeps exhaust paths open and makes components easy to reach. Bundling cables across the exhaust blocks airflow. Overly long cables create slack that tangles and blocks airflow, and removing rear doors reduces physical security without organizing the cables.

prompt: Auditors found that a contractor whose engagement ended three months ago still has an enabled account that can sign in to the data center management portal. Which logical control would best prevent this from happening again?

options.text: A visitor log at the security desk
A geofencing rule that blocks sign-ins from outside the home country
A biometric reader on the data center entrance for all contractors
An IAM process that disables accounts when contracts end

explanation: Identity and access management life cycle processes disable or remove accounts when a person's relationship ends, which closes the gap the auditors found. A biometric reader controls physical entry, not portal sign-ins. A geofencing rule would still allow a former contractor who is in the country, and a visitor log does not affect account status.

prompt: A company's server management portal should only be reachable by administrators who are physically in the corporate offices or the colocation facility. Which logical control uses the device's location to enforce this?

options.text: Geofencing
Faraday cage
Access control vestibule
Badging

explanation: Geofencing allows or blocks access based on a device's geographic location, such as GPS or IP-based position. Badging and access control vestibules are physical entry controls. A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals and does not evaluate location.

prompt: Tailgating has been observed at a data center entrance, where a second person follows a badge holder through the door. Which physical control is designed specifically to stop this?

options.text: A camera that records everyone who walks through the main entrance
A warning sign at the door
A fence with a locked vehicle gate around the parking area outside
An access control vestibule (mantrap)

explanation: An access control vestibule (mantrap) has two interlocking doors, so the inner door opens only after the outer door closes and one authorized person is inside. A camera records tailgating but does not prevent it. A perimeter fence controls a different boundary, and a sign relies on employee behaviour rather than enforcing anything.

prompt: A data center is building a new entrance next to a public road. The security team is concerned that a vehicle could be driven into the building's lobby. Which control addresses this threat?

options.text: Mantrap doors
Bollards
Motion-sensing cameras
Badge readers

explanation: Bollards are short, sturdy posts that stop vehicles from reaching a building entrance while still allowing pedestrians through. Mantrap doors and badge readers control people, and they would not stop a vehicle. Cameras can record an attack but cannot block it.

prompt: A cage at a colocation site requires staff to present a badge and also enter a PIN. The company wants to replace the PIN with a factor that cannot be shared or forgotten. Which factor should it use?

options.text: A second badge issued to each employee for the cage
A fingerprint or palm-vein biometric reader
A physical key for each employee
A longer PIN that is changed every 30 days

explanation: A biometric is something the person is, so it cannot be lent to someone else or forgotten. A second badge and a physical key are both things a person has, which can be shared or lost. A longer PIN is still a knowledge factor that can be shared or forgotten.

prompt: Administrators use a hardware token that displays a code which changes every 30 seconds when they sign in to the hypervisor management console. Which factor category does the token provide?

options.text: Something you have
Something you know
Something you are
Somewhere you are

explanation: A hardware token is a physical device in the user's possession, so it provides a something-you-have factor. A password or PIN is something you know. Biometrics are something you are, and location-based checks such as geofencing are somewhere you are.

prompt: A data center must give vendors temporary access for hardware repairs. The security manager needs to know who is on site at any time, who they are visiting and when they left. Which control provides this?

options.text: Cameras on the loading dock
Shared physical keys stored at the security desk for vendor use
Permanent badges issued to each vendor technician for faster entry
A visitor management system with escorts and temporary badges

explanation: Visitor management records each visitor's identity, host, arrival and departure, and pairs this with escorts and expiring badges. Permanent badges give ongoing access that is not needed for occasional repairs. Shared keys cannot be traced to a person, and cameras alone do not record who a visitor is visiting or when they signed out.

prompt: A server room uses traditional metal keys. A technician who had a key left the company and did not return it. Which weakness of keys does this situation show?

options.text: Keys require network connectivity to the access control server to work
Keys record every entry automatically, which creates privacy concerns
Keys are a biometric factor that can be spoofed
A lost key cannot be disabled, so the lock must be rekeyed

explanation: Unlike a badge that can be disabled centrally, an unreturned key keeps working until the lock is rekeyed or replaced, and keys leave no audit trail. Keys do not use the network and do not log entries. Keys are a possession factor, not a biometric.

prompt: A company is building a secure facility for servers that process classified signals data and must stop electromagnetic emanations from leaving the room and outside signals from entering. Which architectural reinforcement should be used?

options.text: A Faraday cage
Camouflage of the building exterior
Bollards around the building perimeter
An access control vestibule at the entrance

explanation: A Faraday cage is a conductive enclosure that blocks electromagnetic fields, preventing emanations from leaking out and outside signals from getting in. Camouflage hides the facility's purpose but does not block signals. Bollards and vestibules stop vehicles and tailgaters, not radio frequency energy.

prompt: A company's new data center is built in an industrial park. The security team wants the building to attract as little attention as possible. Which approach applies architectural camouflage?

options.text: Paint the fences in the company's brand colors
Place large signs with the company logo at each entrance to deter intruders
List the facility's address and purpose on the company's public website
Use an unmarked, plain exterior with no company signage or logos

explanation: Camouflage makes the facility look like an ordinary building, so an unmarked exterior without signage reduces its profile as a target. Logo signs, branded fences and publishing the address all advertise the facility's purpose. Fences are useful controls, but branding them works against camouflage.

prompt: A security guard reports that a person in a contractor vest asked to be let into the data hall because he forgot his badge. What should the guard do according to good physical security practice?

options.text: Let the person in, because the contractor vest shows they work for an approved vendor
Deny entry until identity and authorization are verified
Let them in with an employee watching
Let the person in and ask them to send the badge number to security later that day

explanation: Guards must verify identity and authorization before granting access, typically through the visitor or temporary-badge process, because a vest or uniform is easy to fake. Letting the person in and following up later defeats the purpose of access control. An informal watcher is not an authorized escort and does not confirm the person should be there.

prompt: A company is designing layered physical security for a new data center. Which three controls add useful layers? (Choose three.)

options.text: Install a perimeter fence with a controlled gate
Assign a single shared PIN to all employees for the data hall door
Install cameras covering entrances and rack aisles with retained footage
Disable badge reader logging to reduce storage use
Require badge access at each data hall door

explanation: Cameras with retained footage, a fenced and gated perimeter, and badge readers at each hall door each add a separate layer of deterrence, prevention or detection. A shared PIN cannot be traced to an individual and is easily passed around. Disabling badge logging removes the audit trail needed for investigations.

prompt: An administrator suspects that someone tried to guess passwords on a Windows file server overnight. Which log should be checked first for failed sign-in events?

options.text: The Setup log
The System log
The Security log
The Application log

explanation: Windows records audited sign-in attempts, including failed logons (event ID 4625), in the Security log. The System log records events from Windows components such as drivers and services. The Application log holds events written by applications, and the Setup log records installation and update events.

prompt: A company runs 60 Linux and Windows servers. After a breach, investigators found that the attacker had cleared the local logs on the compromised servers. Which strategy would have preserved the evidence?

options.text: Rotate local logs more often and compress the older files
Enable verbose debug logging for every application on the servers
Increase the maximum size of each server's local log files
Forward logs in near real time to a central log server or SIEM

explanation: Centralized logging copies events off each server as they happen, so clearing local logs does not erase the copies an attacker cannot reach. Larger local logs and more frequent rotation still keep the only copy on the compromised server. Debug logging adds volume but is just as easy to clear.

prompt: A web server's CPU normally runs at 25-35% during business hours. Monitoring now shows 80% sustained CPU with no change in request volume. What makes it possible to recognize this as abnormal?

options.text: A performance baseline for that server
The server vendor's maximum rated CPU frequency
A single CPU reading taken during the incident
The server's hardware compatibility list entry

explanation: A baseline records what normal looks like for that server, so deviations such as 80% CPU at unchanged load stand out. The vendor's rated frequency says nothing about normal workload. A single reading has nothing to compare against, and the HCL lists supported hardware, not performance norms.

prompt: A capacity planner wants to know whether a database server can handle month-end processing. Which metric collection approach gives the most useful data?

options.text: Capture metrics during both heavy-load month-end periods and light-load periods
Capture metrics only overnight, when the database server is idle
Capture metrics only once, during the first hour after a reboot
Capture metrics only from the hypervisor host, not the database VM

explanation: Comparing heavy-load and light-load metrics shows how the server behaves at its peak and how much headroom remains. Overnight-only data misses the peak. Data from the hour after a reboot is not representative, and host-only metrics hide what is happening inside the database VM.

prompt: A storage volume has grown from 60% to 82% full over the last six months at a steady rate. What is the most useful action for the administrator to take with this data?

options.text: Delete the oldest files on the volume until it returns to 60% full
Project the trend to forecast when the volume will be full
Reset the monitoring counters so the chart starts again from zero
Ignore the growth, because the volume is still below 90% full today

explanation: Trend analysis turns steady growth into a forecast, giving time to add capacity before the volume fills. Ignoring the trend risks an outage. Deleting files without a retention decision may destroy needed data, and resetting counters only removes the history.

prompt:
Users report that a Linux application server is slow. The administrator runs a command and sees:

MiB Mem :  15890.4 total,    212.7 free,  15301.2 used,    376.5 buff/cache
MiB Swap:   4096.0 total,    118.3 free,   3977.7 used.     281.0 avail Mem

Which resource is the likely bottleneck?

options.text: CPU, because the buff/cache figure shows the processors are overloaded
Network, because the available memory figure reflects socket buffers
Disk capacity, because the swap total is smaller than the installed RAM
Memory, because RAM is nearly exhausted and almost all swap is in use

explanation: The output shows only about 281 MiB of memory available and nearly 4 GiB of swap used, so the server is paging heavily and memory is the bottleneck. Buff/cache is memory used for caching, not a CPU measure. The swap size relative to RAM is a configuration choice, and available memory does not measure network load.

prompt: An administrator sees the following on a Windows server's Resource Monitor during a slowdown: disk queue length on the data volume averages 25, while CPU is at 15% and memory is 40% used. Which utilization area should be investigated?

options.text: CPU
Memory
Disk I/O
Network traffic

explanation: A sustained disk queue far above the number of spindles or the array's capacity means requests are waiting for storage, so disk I/O is the constraint. CPU at 15% and memory at 40% leave plenty of headroom. Nothing in the data points to network saturation.

prompt: A monitoring system detects that a production database server's disk is 95% full at 2 a.m. The on-call administrator must be notified immediately even if not at a computer. Which alerting method fits best?

options.text: A weekly email report summarizing disk usage
A message posted to a team channel read during business hours
An entry in the monitoring dashboard's event list
A page or SMS to the on-call administrator's phone

explanation: Pager or SMS alerts reach the on-call person immediately wherever they are, which suits an urgent overnight condition. A dashboard entry requires someone to be watching. A weekly report and a business-hours channel both delay the response for hours.

prompt: A managed service provider monitors a customer's servers. When a critical server goes down, both the provider's engineers and the customer's IT manager must be told. How should alerting be configured?

options.text: Write the alerts to the server's local event log for both teams to review later
Send alerts only to the customer contact and let them forward alerts to the provider
Send internal alerts to the provider and external alerts to the customer
Send alerts only to the provider's on-call team and let the customer find out from users

explanation: Separating internal and external alert recipients means the responders are paged and the customer is informed directly. Alerting only one party leaves the other uninformed or delays the response. Local logs are not notifications and may be unreachable when the server is down.

prompt: A team lead wants a single screen in the operations center that shows CPU, memory, disk and network utilization for all critical servers, with color-coded status. What should be built?

options.text: A runbook for each server
A configuration management database
A centralized syslog server
A monitoring dashboard

explanation: A dashboard aggregates metrics and status for many systems into one visual view for at-a-glance monitoring. A syslog server stores log messages but does not present utilization at a glance. A CMDB tracks configuration items, and runbooks document procedures.

prompt: A rack server in a data center has no network connectivity and its BMC is not configured. The administrator needs a monitor, keyboard and mouse at the rack to work on it. What should be brought to the rack?

options.text: A crash cart
A cable tester
A digital thermometer
A loopback plug

explanation: A crash cart is a mobile cart with a monitor, keyboard and mouse that can be plugged directly into a server for local console access. A digital thermometer measures temperature. A cable tester checks cabling, and a loopback plug tests a port, but neither provides console access.

prompt: A server keeps throttling its CPUs, and the administrator suspects the cold aisle supply air in that row is warmer than the facility monitoring reports. Which tool lets the administrator verify the intake temperature at the server's front panel?

options.text: A tone generator
A multimeter
A crash cart
A digital thermometer

explanation: A digital (often infrared or probe) thermometer measures the actual air temperature at the server intake. A multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance. A tone generator traces cables, and a crash cart provides console access, not temperature readings.

prompt: A server shows an amber LED and a two-digit code on its front diagnostic panel. The administrator does not recognize the code. Which resource should be checked to interpret it?

options.text: The output of an nmap scan of the BMC
The operating system's event log
The hypervisor's resource allocation settings
The server's service manual

explanation: Front-panel LED and diagnostic codes are vendor-specific, and the server's service manual lists what each code means. The OS event log may not record hardware codes, especially if the server will not boot. An nmap scan shows open ports, and hypervisor settings do not explain hardware codes.

prompt: An administrator needs to confirm that a new Linux server is listening only on TCP ports 22 and 443 before it goes into production. Which tool, run from another host, would check this?

options.text: tracert
nmap
arp
nslookup

explanation: nmap scans a host to report which TCP and UDP ports are open, closed or filtered. nslookup queries DNS. tracert shows the routers along a path, and arp displays the IP-to-MAC address cache.

prompt: A Windows administrator wants to check whether a remote SQL server is reachable on TCP port 1433 without installing extra software. Which command should be used?

options.text: tnc sql01 -Port 1433
nslookup sql01 1433
tracert -p 1433 sql01
ping sql01 -n 1433

explanation: tnc is the built-in PowerShell alias for Test-NetConnection, and the -Port parameter tests a TCP connection to the given port. ping -n sets the number of echo requests and uses ICMP, not TCP. tracert has no port option, and the second nslookup argument is the DNS server to query, not a port.

prompt: A Windows server shows an unexpected outbound connection to an unfamiliar IP address. The administrator wants a graphical view of every TCP and UDP endpoint along with the process that owns it. Which tool provides this?

options.text: mstsc
TCPView
DiskPart
Notepad

explanation: TCPView, a Sysinternals tool, lists all TCP and UDP endpoints with their local and remote addresses, state and owning process. Notepad is a text editor. DiskPart manages disks and partitions, and mstsc is the Remote Desktop client.

prompt:
An administrator runs the following command from a Linux host:

$ dig +short www.example.com

What information does the command return?

options.text: The MAC address of the web server on the local segment
The HTTP response headers that the web server returns
The routers on the path between the host and the web server
The IP addresses (or CNAME) that DNS returns for the name

explanation: dig queries DNS, and +short prints just the answer records such as A records or a CNAME. Path routers are shown by traceroute. HTTP headers are retrieved with curl -I, and MAC addresses on the local segment are shown in the ARP or neighbour table.

prompt: An administrator wants to verify that a web API on a Linux server returns an HTTP 200 status and inspect its response headers from the command line. Which tool should be used?

options.text: ping
curl
df
telnet

explanation: curl sends HTTP requests and, with options such as -I or -v, shows the status code and response headers. telnet can open a raw TCP connection but does not interpret HTTP for you. ping only tests ICMP reachability, and df reports filesystem space.

prompt: A downloaded firmware image must be checked against the vendor's published SHA-256 value before it is flashed to a server. Which command on a Windows server performs this check?

options.text: diskpart /s .\fw.bin
chkdsk .\fw.bin /f
Get-FileHash .\fw.bin -Algorithm SHA256
dir .\fw.bin /s

explanation: Get-FileHash computes a file's hash, and SHA256 is its default algorithm, so the output can be compared with the vendor's value. chkdsk checks a volume's file system, not a file's integrity against a published hash. diskpart /s runs a script of DiskPart commands, and dir lists files without hashing them.

prompt: A Linux server reports 'No space left on device' when writing to /var. Which command shows the used and available space on each mounted filesystem?

options.text: fdisk -l
ls -la /var
df -h
top

explanation: df -h reports size, used and available space for each mounted filesystem in human-readable units. fdisk -l lists partition tables but not filesystem usage. ls -la lists files in a directory without totals for the filesystem, and top shows processes, CPU and memory.

prompt: A RAID controller reports that a member drive has crossed a SMART threshold for reallocated sectors, but the drive is still online and the array is optimal. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Replace the drive soon, while the array is still redundant
Wait for the drive to fail completely, since the array is still optimal
Remove the drive from the array to stop the predictive failure warnings
Run a full low-level format on the drive to clear its SMART counters

explanation: A predictive failure alert means the drive is likely to fail soon, so replacing it while redundancy is intact avoids running degraded or losing data if a second drive fails. Waiting gives up that safety margin. Formatting does not reset SMART attributes or fix failing media, and pulling the drive degrades the array for no benefit.

prompt: After installing new memory modules from a spare-parts bin, a server that uses RDIMMs fails POST with a memory configuration error. The new modules are the correct capacity and speed. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The new modules are ECC DIMMs, which cannot be mixed with registered DIMMs
The modules are a faster speed than required, which a server cannot downclock
The CMOS battery must be replaced before any new memory will be detected
The new modules are unbuffered DIMMs, which cannot be mixed with registered DIMMs

explanation: Registered and unbuffered DIMMs use different signaling and cannot be mixed in the same system, which causes POST memory errors. RDIMMs in servers are normally ECC, so ECC is not the conflict. Faster DIMMs are typically run at the slower supported speed, and the CMOS battery does not control memory detection.

prompt: A Windows server stops with a blue screen showing MEMORY_MANAGEMENT, and the system event log shows corrected memory errors on the same DIMM slot over the past week. What should the administrator do next?

options.text: Replace the DIMM in the reported slot and keep monitoring for errors
Disable ECC in the firmware so that corrected errors are no longer logged
Increase the page file size so that Windows uses less physical memory
Reinstall the operating system, because the blue screen indicates OS corruption

explanation: Repeated corrected errors on one slot followed by a memory-related stop error point to a failing DIMM, which should be replaced. Reinstalling the OS does not fix faulty hardware. A larger page file does not stop bad memory from being used, and disabling ECC would turn correctable errors into silent corruption or crashes.

prompt: A VMware ESXi host halts and displays a purple diagnostic screen that mentions an uncorrectable machine check exception. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The vCenter Server lost network connection to the host
A datastore on the host has run out of free space
A hardware fault such as failing memory or CPU
A guest VM's application crashed and stopped responding

explanation: The purple diagnostic screen is ESXi's host-level crash screen, and an uncorrectable machine check exception reports a hardware error, commonly memory or CPU. A guest application crash does not halt the host. Losing the vCenter connection or filling a datastore causes alarms, not a host crash.

prompt: A Linux server rebooted unexpectedly, and kdump was configured beforehand. Why is the resulting memory dump useful?

options.text: It restores the running processes to their state before the crash
It saves kernel memory at the crash so the cause can be analyzed
It resets the system firmware to defaults to prevent another crash
It replaces the failed memory modules with spare capacity from swap

explanation: A memory dump saves the contents of kernel memory at the time of the crash so that tools such as the crash utility can find the failing driver or hardware. It does not restore processes. It has no ability to replace hardware or reset firmware settings.

prompt: A server that has been in storage for several years loses its date and time and boot order every time it is unplugged. Which component should be replaced?

options.text: The UEFI firmware chip
The power supply unit
The RAID controller's cache battery
The CMOS battery on the system board

explanation: The CMOS battery keeps the real-time clock and firmware settings when the server has no power, so lost time and settings after unplugging point to a dead battery. The cache battery protects RAID controller write cache, not firmware settings. A failed power supply would stop the server from running, and firmware settings loss is not a sign of a bad firmware chip.

prompt: A RAID controller log shows 'Battery charge low; cache policy changed from Write-Back to Write-Through.' Users report slower database writes. What is the cause of the slowdown?

options.text: The controller increased the stripe size, which slows small random writes
The controller switched the array to RAID 0 to save battery power
Write-back caching was disabled because the battery is low
The controller started a background rebuild of the array after a drive failure

explanation: When the cache battery cannot protect cached data during a power loss, the controller falls back to write-through, so writes wait for the disks and performance drops. The log does not mention a rebuild. Controllers do not change stripe size or RAID level on their own.

prompt: A technician walking past a rack notices a burning smell and a high-pitched whine coming from one server's power supply area. What should be done first?

options.text: Shut down the affected server safely and remove the power supply for inspection
Ignore the noise, because power supply fans often whine under normal load
Spray the area with water to cool the power supply before investigating it
Open the power supply casing while the server runs to locate the source

explanation: A burning smell with an electrical whine suggests a failing component, so the server should be shut down and the part removed before it causes damage or a fire. Water is dangerous on electrical equipment. Ignoring a burning smell risks a fire, and power supplies contain hazardous voltages and should never be opened, especially while running.

prompt: A server does not display video, but it emits a repeating pattern of beeps during startup. What is the best way to use this information?

options.text: Clear all event logs on the server, because beeps mean the logs are full
Reinstall the operating system, because beeps indicate a corrupted bootloader
Replace the monitor cable, because beeps always mean a video cable problem
Look up the beep pattern in the vendor's documentation

explanation: POST beep codes are vendor-specific signals that identify which component failed the power-on self-test, and the vendor's documentation decodes them. POST runs before the bootloader, so the OS is not involved. Beeps can indicate many failures, not only video, and they have nothing to do with full logs.

prompt:
A GPU server running training jobs shows the following in its monitoring output, and jobs have become noticeably slower:

GPU 0: Temp 91 C  Clocks: throttled (HW thermal slowdown)
GPU 1: Temp 64 C  Clocks: normal

What is the most likely issue?

options.text: GPU 1 is failing, because its temperature is much lower than GPU 0
The training software is limiting GPU 0 to save electricity at night
GPU 0 is overheating and reducing its clock speed to protect itself
GPU 0 has a memory leak in the training job that is raising its temperature

explanation: The output shows GPU 0 at 91 C with a hardware thermal slowdown flag, meaning it is throttling to avoid damage, which slows jobs. A lower temperature on GPU 1 is normal, not a failure sign. Thermal slowdown is a hardware protection, not a software power policy, and a memory leak does not cause heat throttling.

prompt: Several servers in one rack report high inlet and component temperatures, while other racks in the room are normal. Which three are likely causes? (Choose three.)

options.text: Running the server on 240 VAC instead of 120 VAC
Dust buildup on the server's front intake filters
Using RDIMMs instead of UDIMMs
Blocked or missing blanking panels in the rack
A failed fan in the server chassis

explanation: Missing blanking panels let hot exhaust recirculate to the front of the rack, a failed fan reduces airflow, and dust on intake filters restricts cooling air. RDIMMs are the normal memory type in servers and do not cause overheating. Running at 240 VAC slightly improves power supply efficiency and does not cause high temperatures.

prompt: A Windows application server becomes slow every few days and recovers only after a reboot. Performance Monitor shows that one service's Private Bytes counter climbs steadily from 400 MB to 11 GB between reboots, while user load stays the same. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A fragmented page file on the system volume
An expired TLS certificate on the service's endpoint
A memory leak in that service
A failing DIMM that is reducing the installed memory

explanation: Memory that a process allocates and never releases grows steadily regardless of load until a restart frees it, which is the pattern of a memory leak. A failing DIMM causes errors or crashes rather than one process's steady growth. Page file fragmentation does not increase a process's private bytes, and an expired certificate causes connection errors, not memory growth.

prompt: After an unexpected power loss, a Windows server boots, but several built-in tools fail with errors about missing or damaged system files. Which command should the administrator run first to verify and repair protected system files?

options.text: sfc /scannow
bcdedit /enum
chkdsk /r
diskpart clean

explanation: System File Checker (sfc /scannow) scans protected Windows system files and replaces corrupted ones from the component store; DISM /RestoreHealth can repair the store if SFC cannot. chkdsk /r checks the file system and disk surface but does not restore Windows system files. diskpart clean erases a disk's partition information, and bcdedit /enum only lists boot configuration entries.

prompt: After a technician added a new disk and changed the firmware boot settings, a Linux server reports 'No bootable device' at startup. The OS disk is healthy and shows up in the firmware's device list. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The root password expired, so the kernel refuses to load at startup
The new disk is missing an NTFS partition that the Linux bootloader needs
The network bonding configuration on the server has become corrupted
The firmware boot order now tries the new, empty disk instead of the OS disk

explanation: If the firmware tries to boot from the new disk, which has no bootloader, it reports that no bootable device was found even though the OS disk is fine. An expired password affects logon after the OS loads. Network bonding is configured long after the bootloader runs, and Linux does not need an NTFS partition to boot.

prompt: Users cannot sign in to a domain-joined Windows server, and its System log shows Kerberos errors. Running w32tm /query /status shows the server's clock is 9 minutes behind the domain controller. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Increase the Kerberos maximum ticket lifetime to 24 hours on the server
Resynchronize the server's clock with the domain time hierarchy
Disable Kerberos so the server falls back to local accounts only
Rejoin the server to the domain using a new computer account name

explanation: Kerberos rejects authentication when clocks differ by more than the allowed skew, 5 minutes by default, so correcting time synchronization fixes the logons. Rejoining the domain does not fix the clock. Ticket lifetime is unrelated to clock skew, and disabling Kerberos would break domain authentication.

prompt:
An administrator tries to connect to an old network appliance from a current Linux server and gets:

Unable to negotiate with 10.10.4.20 port 22: no matching key exchange method found. Their offer: diffie-hellman-group1-sha1

What is the cause?

options.text: A firewall between the hosts is blocking TCP port 22
The administrator typed the wrong password for the appliance
The appliance's SSH host key changed since the last connection
The client and appliance have no key exchange algorithm in common

explanation: The message shows the appliance offers only a legacy key exchange method that the modern client has disabled, an encryption negotiation mismatch; the long-term fix is updating the appliance. A changed host key produces a host identification warning instead. A wrong password fails after negotiation, and a blocked port would cause a timeout or refused connection rather than a negotiation error.

prompt: After a change to an Apache web server configuration file, the service fails to start. Which step most directly identifies the configuration error?

options.text: Reboot the server repeatedly until the web service starts on its own
Reinstall the operating system to restore the default configuration
Run the configuration syntax test and read the service's logs
Increase the server's RAM so that the service has room to load

explanation: A syntax test (for example apachectl configtest) and the service's log entries point to the exact line and directive that broke the configuration. Rebooting does not change a bad configuration. Reinstalling the OS is drastic and unnecessary, and memory is not the problem when a configuration file has an error.

prompt: A user can sign in to every server except one Windows file server, where the error says the sign-in method is not allowed. Other members of the same group can sign in. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The file server's network cable has failed and it is offline
The user's account is not granted the logon right for that server
The user's password has expired across the whole domain
The domain controller's DNS zone is missing the user's record

explanation: A message that the sign-in method is not allowed indicates a missing logon right, such as Allow log on locally or through Remote Desktop Services, for that account on that server. An expired password would affect every server. A failed cable would stop all users, and user accounts do not have DNS records.

prompt: A line-of-business application on a Windows server stops responding, and Task Manager shows it as 'Not responding' with no CPU use. Other applications work normally. What should the administrator try first?

options.text: Reformat the system volume and restore the server from backup
End the hung process, restart the application and review its logs
Disable the server's antivirus software permanently
Replace the server's power supply to rule out power problems

explanation: Ending the hung process and restarting the application restores service, and the application's logs help find why it hung. Reformatting and restoring the server is far out of proportion. A power supply problem would affect the whole server, and permanently disabling antivirus weakens security without evidence.

prompt: A virtual machine's applications have become slow. Inside the guest, CPU usage is only 30%, but the hypervisor shows high CPU ready time for the VM. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The host's physical CPUs are oversubscribed
The VM's virtual disk is formatted with the wrong file system
The VM's network adapter is set to a lower speed than the host
The guest OS has too many idle background services installed

explanation: High CPU ready time means the VM is ready to run but waiting for a physical CPU, a sign of too many vCPUs competing on the host. Idle services do not create ready time. The guest file system and virtual NIC link speed do not affect CPU scheduling on the host.

prompt: After updating the NIC driver on a Windows server, the adapter drops its connection every few minutes. The previous driver was stable. What is the quickest way to restore stability?

options.text: Install a second operating system on the server to compare behaviour
Replace the network switch the server is connected to
Roll back the NIC driver to the previous version in Device Manager
Disable the network adapter permanently and use Wi-Fi

explanation: Because the problem started right after the driver update, rolling back to the previously stable driver is the quickest fix while the new version is investigated. A second OS install does not solve the problem. The switch worked before the change, and Wi-Fi is not an appropriate server connection.

prompt: A Red Hat Enterprise Linux server shows application errors immediately after a dnf update transaction. The administrator wants to reverse just that transaction. Which command does this?

options.text: dnf history undo <transaction-id>
dnf makecache
dnf clean all
rpm --rebuilddb

explanation: dnf history undo reverses the actions of a specific transaction listed in dnf history, such as reinstalling the previous package versions. dnf clean all removes cached metadata and packages. dnf makecache downloads repository metadata, and rpm --rebuilddb rebuilds the RPM database without changing installed packages.

prompt: A Windows server's cumulative update fails repeatedly with an installation error. Which three are common causes to check? (Choose three.)

options.text: A pending restart from an earlier update
Insufficient free disk space on the system volume
A user's desktop wallpaper policy
A corrupted component store or update cache
An incorrect screen resolution setting

explanation: Updates often fail when the system volume lacks free space, when an earlier update is still waiting for a restart, or when the component store or update cache is corrupted. Screen resolution and wallpaper policies have no effect on update installation.

prompt:
An administrator checks a Linux server with software RAID and sees:

$ cat /proc/mdstat
md0 : active raid1 sdb1[1] sda1[0](F)
      976630464 blocks super 1.2 [2/1] [_U]

What is the state of the array?

options.text: The mirror is degraded because sda1 has failed, and only sdb1 is active
The mirror is healthy, because both member disks are still listed in it
The mirror is rebuilding onto sda1, which is a newly added spare disk
The mirror has failed completely and the md0 device is now read-only

explanation: The (F) flag marks sda1 as failed, and [2/1] [_U] shows that only one of two members is working, so the array is degraded but still running. A rebuild would show a recovery progress line. Being listed does not mean a member is healthy, and the array remains active on sdb1.

prompt: A RAID 5 array of four drives reports one failed drive. A hot spare is not configured. What should the administrator do to restore redundancy?

options.text: Convert the array to RAID 0 so that it uses the remaining drives
Replace the failed drive and let the array rebuild
Remove a second drive so the controller rebalances the array
Initialize the array again so that all four drives are reset

explanation: Replacing the failed member with a compatible drive starts a rebuild that restores parity protection. Initializing the array erases its data. Converting to RAID 0 removes redundancy entirely, and removing a second drive from a degraded RAID 5 array causes it to fail.

prompt: A RAID controller reports that its flash-backed cache module has failed, and the controller has switched all virtual disks to write-through. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Replace the cache backup module so write-back caching can be safely re-enabled
Replace every drive in the array, since the cache failure damaged them
Rebuild each virtual disk from scratch to reset the cache policy
Force write-back caching on without replacing the module to restore speed

explanation: Replacing the failed cache backup (battery or supercapacitor and flash) restores protection for cached writes, after which the controller can return to write-back. Forcing write-back without protection risks losing data on a power failure. The drives are not affected, and rebuilding virtual disks does not fix a failed cache module.

prompt:
A Linux server's application logs show 'No space left on device', yet the administrator sees this:

$ df -h /var
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sdb1        50G   19G   29G  40% /var

Which command should be run next?

options.text: free -h, to check whether the server has run out of physical memory
ip addr show, to check whether the network interface is configured
df -i /var, to check whether the filesystem has run out of inodes
fdisk -l /dev/sdb, to check whether the partition table is damaged

explanation: A filesystem can report 'No space left on device' when all inodes are used, often by millions of small files, even with free blocks; df -i shows inode use. The partition table does not cause this error on a mounted filesystem. Memory and network configuration are unrelated to filesystem space.

prompt: An administrator installed four new drives in a server that has a hardware RAID controller. The operating system does not show any new disks. The controller's utility lists the drives as 'Unconfigured Good'. What should be done?

options.text: Replace the drives, because 'Unconfigured Good' means they have failed
Install a newer graphics driver so the OS can detect the drives
Create a virtual disk or set the drives to non-RAID mode
Format the drives with NTFS from the server's firmware setup

explanation: Drives behind a hardware RAID controller are not presented to the OS until they are part of a virtual disk or passed through as non-RAID/JBOD devices. Graphics drivers have nothing to do with storage. Firmware setup does not format drives with NTFS, and 'Unconfigured Good' means the drives are healthy but unassigned.

prompt: Database write latency on a server has doubled. The administrator runs iostat and sees that one member disk of a RAID 10 array shows an average wait time of 180 ms while the other members show 4 ms. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The database is using too little memory, which raises disk wait times
The server's NIC is saturated, which slows down local disk writes
The array has too few members for RAID 10, so it is waiting on parity
That member disk is failing or slow and is dragging down the array

explanation: In an array, one slow or failing member delays every write that touches it, so a single disk with much higher wait times is the likely culprit. RAID 10 does not use parity. Memory pressure would raise I/O across all disks rather than one, and NIC saturation does not affect local disk latency.

prompt:
The kernel log on a Linux file server shows repeated entries like the following for one disk:

blk_update_request: I/O error, dev sdc, sector 1953104
Buffer I/O error on dev sdc1, logical block 244138

What should the administrator do?

options.text: Delete the file at that sector so the error messages will stop
Back up the disk's data, check SMART and cabling, and plan a replacement
Increase the filesystem's block size so the bad sector is skipped
Ignore the messages, because the kernel retries and corrects all I/O errors

explanation: Repeated read/write errors on one device point to failing media, a bad cable or a controller problem, so data should be protected and the hardware checked and replaced. The kernel does not correct failing media. Changing block size requires reformatting and does not remove bad sectors, and deleting a file does not repair the disk.

prompt: An administrator plugs a USB backup drive into a Windows server. The drive appears in Disk Management as healthy with a partition, but no drive letter appears in File Explorer. What should be done?

options.text: Run diskpart clean on the drive and create a new partition
Assign a drive letter to the partition in Disk Management
Replace the USB drive, because it has a hardware fault
Convert the disk to a dynamic disk so Windows can mount it

explanation: A healthy partition without a drive letter is not shown in File Explorer, and assigning a letter (or mount point) makes it accessible. Converting to dynamic disk is not needed and is unsuitable for removable drives. diskpart clean erases the drive's data, and a drive that shows a healthy partition is not faulty.

prompt: On a Linux server, files that a script wrote to /data during the night are missing this morning. The administrator finds that the SAN volume normally mounted on /data was not mounted overnight and was remounted at 7 a.m. Where are the missing files most likely located?

options.text: On the root filesystem, in the /data directory now hidden under the mount
In the /tmp directory, where the kernel redirects failed writes
In the system's swap partition, where unmounted writes are stored
On the SAN volume, in a hidden lost+found directory after a rebuild

explanation: While the SAN volume was unmounted, the script wrote into the empty /data directory on the root filesystem; mounting the volume over it hides those files until it is unmounted or the directory is bind-mounted elsewhere. lost+found holds orphaned files from a filesystem check. Swap is not used for file storage, and the kernel does not redirect writes to /tmp.

prompt: After a BIOS firmware update, a Windows server stops at the BitLocker recovery screen and asks for a recovery key. What most likely caused this, and how can it be avoided next time?

options.text: The firmware change altered TPM measurements; suspend BitLocker before firmware updates
The update erased the drive's encryption; re-encrypt the drive after each firmware update
The CMOS battery failed during the update; replace the battery before each update
The boot volume was corrupted; run chkdsk before each firmware update

explanation: BitLocker seals its key to TPM measurements of the boot chain, so a firmware update can trigger recovery; suspending protection before the update and resuming after avoids it. The drive is still encrypted, which is why it asks for the key. A CMOS battery failure and file system corruption do not produce a BitLocker recovery prompt in this way.

prompt:
A ZFS pool reports checksum errors on one disk after a scrub:

  NAME        STATE     READ WRITE CKSUM
  tank        ONLINE       0     0     0
    mirror-0  ONLINE       0     0     0
      sda     ONLINE       0     0    14
      sdb     ONLINE       0     0     0

What does this indicate?

options.text: ZFS detected corrupted blocks on sda and repaired them from the mirror copy on sdb
Both disks hold corrupted data, and the pool must be restored from a backup
The sdb disk has failed, because it shows zero errors in every column
The pool has run out of space, and the scrub could not finish checking it

explanation: ZFS checksums every block, so a scrub finds silent corruption on sda and repairs it from the good copy on sdb; repeated errors mean sda should be checked or replaced. The pool and mirror show no errors, so data is intact. Zero errors on sdb means it is healthy, and checksum errors do not indicate a full pool.

prompt: A restore of last week's backup of a file server fails with an error that the backup set is encrypted and the key cannot be found. The backup job was configured by an administrator who has since left. What does this show about the backup process?

options.text: Backups should never be encrypted, because encryption always prevents restores
Backup encryption keys must be escrowed and documented separately
Incremental backups should be replaced with full backups to avoid key problems
Restores should be done only by the administrator who set up the backup job

explanation: Encrypted backups are only usable if the keys are escrowed and documented, so losing the key makes the data unrecoverable; regular restore tests would have found this earlier. Encryption is a good practice for backups when keys are managed. Relying on one person is the weakness here, and the backup type does not change the need for a key.

prompt: A file server's users report that documents in a shared folder now have a new '.locked' extension and cannot be opened, and a text file demanding payment has appeared in each folder. What should the administrator do first?

options.text: Restore the latest backup over the infected server immediately
Run a disk defragmentation to recover the original file contents
Isolate the server from the network to stop the encryption from spreading
Rename the files back to their original extension so users can open them

explanation: Unexpected encryption with a ransom note indicates ransomware, and isolating the server limits further encryption and spread before investigation and recovery. Renaming files does not decrypt them. Defragmentation cannot recover encrypted content, and restoring before the threat is contained and the backup is verified clean can lead to reinfection.

prompt: A new Windows server cannot join the corp.example.com Active Directory domain. The error says that a domain controller for the domain could not be contacted. The server can ping the domain controller by IP address. Its IP configuration lists 8.8.8.8 as the only DNS server. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Disable the server's firewall completely and retry the domain join
Add a static route to the domain controller and retry the domain join
Create a computer account for the server in a different OU and retry
Set the server's DNS to the domain's internal DNS servers and retry the join

explanation: Domain join locates domain controllers through SRV records in the domain's DNS, which a public resolver cannot provide, so pointing the server at internal DNS fixes the problem. Routing works, since the DC answers pings. The OU of a precreated account does not affect locating a DC, and disabling the firewall is unnecessary and unsafe.

prompt:
A Linux server sends this output when the administrator checks its address:

$ ip -4 addr show eth0
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500
    inet 169.254.37.112/16 scope link eth0

What does the address indicate?

options.text: The server's network cable is unplugged, so the kernel disabled the interface
The server has an IPv6 address that is being displayed in IPv4 notation
No DHCP server answered, so it self-assigned a link-local address
The server received a valid lease from the DHCP server on a reserved private range

explanation: Addresses in 169.254.0.0/16 are link-local (APIPA) addresses that hosts assign themselves when no DHCP server responds, so the DHCP path needs checking. A DHCP lease would come from the scope's configured range. The interface shows UP and LOWER_UP, so the link is connected, and the address is genuine IPv4.

prompt: Several servers on a new VLAN fail to get DHCP addresses, while servers on other VLANs work. The DHCP server is on a different subnet. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: No DHCP relay (IP helper) is configured on the new VLAN's router interface
The servers on the new VLAN have duplicate MAC addresses assigned
The DNS zone for the new VLAN lacks a reverse lookup zone
The DHCP server's scope options are missing a default gateway entry

explanation: DHCP discovery uses broadcasts that do not cross routers, so a VLAN whose DHCP server is on another subnet needs a relay agent on its gateway. A missing gateway option would still give clients an address. Duplicate MACs across all new servers is very unlikely, and reverse DNS zones do not affect DHCP leases.

prompt:
Two servers intermittently lose connectivity, and the administrator sees the following ARP entries on a third host at different times:

10.20.5.40  00-50-56-a1-3c-10  dynamic
10.20.5.40  00-50-56-a1-77-e2  dynamic

What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The default gateway has failed and is answering with random MACs
Two devices are configured with the same IP address, 10.20.5.40
The ARP cache on the third host is full and is overwriting entries
One of the servers has two NICs that are bonded in active-backup mode

explanation: The same IP mapping to two different MAC addresses at different times is the signature of an IP address conflict, which causes the intermittent loss. An ARP cache does not invent different MACs for one address. Active-backup bonding normally keeps a single MAC for the bond, and a failed gateway would not answer at all.

prompt:
A server's gigabit link is very slow and drops occasionally. The administrator runs ethtool and sees:

Speed: 100Mb/s
Duplex: Full
Link detected: yes

The switch port and NIC both support 1000 Mb/s with auto-negotiation. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A missing default gateway, which limits traffic to the local subnet
A full ARP table on the switch, which limits the link negotiation speed
A damaged patch cable with a faulty wire pair
A DNS misconfiguration that slows down name lookups for the server

explanation: Gigabit Ethernet uses all four pairs while 100 Mb/s needs only two, so a broken or poor pair often makes the link negotiate down and drop; replacing the cable is the fix. DNS problems do not change link speed. A missing gateway affects routing, not negotiation, and ARP tables have no effect on physical link speed.

prompt:
A Linux server can reach hosts on its own subnet but not on any other subnet. The administrator runs:

$ ip route
10.30.8.0/24 dev ens192 proto kernel scope link src 10.30.8.25

What is wrong?

options.text: The server has no default route to its gateway
The server has a duplicate IP address on the network
The server's subnet mask is too large for the network
The server's interface is configured for the wrong VLAN

explanation: The routing table has only the connected subnet route and no 'default via' entry, so traffic to other subnets has nowhere to go. The /24 mask matches the connected network. A wrong VLAN or duplicate IP would also break local communication, which works here.

prompt: An application on a Linux server fails to connect to db01.corp.example.com, but nslookup db01.corp.example.com returns the correct address, 10.40.2.15. Pinging the name from the server goes to 10.40.9.99. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The server's DHCP lease expired and it lost its DNS configuration
The DNS server has a stale record pointing to the old database address
An outdated entry in the server's /etc/hosts file overrides DNS for that name
The database server's firewall is blocking ICMP echo requests

explanation: nslookup queries DNS directly, while ping and most applications use the system resolver, which checks /etc/hosts first by default; a stale hosts entry explains the different address. The DNS server returns the correct address. A firewall blocking ICMP would not change the resolved address, and an expired lease would break nslookup too.

prompt:
A PostgreSQL service on a Linux server is running, but remote application servers cannot connect to it on port 5432. The administrator runs:

$ ss -tlnp | grep 5432
LISTEN 0 244 127.0.0.1:5432 0.0.0.0:* users:(("postgres",pid=1184,fd=6))

What is the cause?

options.text: The service is listening only on the loopback address
The service is listening on UDP instead of TCP for client connections
The service is bound to all addresses, so a router must be blocking it
The service is not running, because no process is listed for port 5432

explanation: The listener is bound to 127.0.0.1, so only local connections are accepted; the listen address must include the server's network interface. A process is listed, so it is running. The -t option shows TCP sockets, and binding to all addresses would show 0.0.0.0 or *, not 127.0.0.1.

prompt: Users can ping a Windows file server by name and IP address, but cannot open \\fs01\data. From a client, Test-NetConnection fs01 -Port 445 reports TcpTestSucceeded: False. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The server's network cable is damaged and drops packets
A firewall is blocking TCP port 445
The clients cannot resolve the server's name in DNS
The clients have APIPA addresses because DHCP has failed

explanation: Pings by name and IP succeed but a TCP test to port 445 fails, so the SMB port is being blocked, typically by a host or network firewall. Name resolution works because pinging by name succeeds. A bad cable or APIPA addressing would break the pings as well.

prompt: Clients cannot reach a web application after a server migration. The administrator finds that the Windows service for the application is set to Manual and is stopped after the reboot. What should be done?

options.text: Change the server's IP address to a different subnet
Reinstall the network driver and restart the server
Add the server's IP address to each client's hosts file
Start the service and set its startup type to Automatic

explanation: A stopped service makes the application unavailable even though the network is fine, and setting it to Automatic ensures it starts after future reboots. Network drivers are not the issue when the service is stopped. Hosts file entries and readdressing do not start the service.

prompt: A newly racked server has no network connectivity. Which three checks help isolate whether the problem is physical, IP routing or name resolution? (Choose three.)

options.text: Run ping to the server's default gateway
Run nslookup for a known internal host name
Run defrag on the server's system volume
Check the switch port and NIC link lights
Run sfc /scannow on the server

explanation: Link lights check the physical layer, pinging the gateway checks IP configuration and local routing, and nslookup checks name resolution. sfc /scannow repairs Windows system files and defrag optimizes disk layout, and neither tests network connectivity.

prompt:
A user cannot sign in to a RHEL server over SSH even after a password reset. The administrator runs:

# faillock --user jdoe
jdoe:
When                Type  Source        Valid
2026-11-20 08:14:02 RHOST 10.8.1.77     V
2026-11-20 08:14:09 RHOST 10.8.1.77     V
2026-11-20 08:14:15 RHOST 10.8.1.77     V

What should the administrator do after confirming the failures came from the user's own workstation?

options.text: Add jdoe to the wheel group so the lockout is bypassed
Run faillock --user jdoe --reset to clear the lockout
Delete and recreate the jdoe account with the same UID
Restart the sshd service to clear all failed login records

explanation: The account is locked by pam_faillock after repeated failures, and faillock --reset clears the recorded failures so the user can sign in. Recreating the account is unnecessary and risks losing settings. Restarting sshd does not clear faillock records, and adding the user to wheel grants admin rights instead of fixing the lockout.

prompt: A user can edit files in D:\Projects when signed in locally to a Windows file server, but over the network through the Projects share can only open them read-only. The NTFS permission is Modify and the share permission is Read. Why?

options.text: The user's local sign-in session is caching an old copy of the NTFS permissions
Share permissions override NTFS permissions whenever they are more permissive
Over the network the more restrictive of share and NTFS permissions applies, so Read wins
NTFS permissions are ignored for network access, so only the share setting applies

explanation: When a share is accessed over the network, Windows evaluates both share and NTFS permissions and the most restrictive result applies, so Read limits the user. NTFS permissions still apply to network access. Share permissions never override NTFS to grant more access, and cached sessions do not explain the difference.

prompt:
During a routine check, an administrator runs this on a Linux web server:

$ ss -tlnp
LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:22    users:(("sshd",pid=812))
LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:443   users:(("nginx",pid=1020))
LISTEN 0 5   0.0.0.0:4444  users:(("python3",pid=29981))

The server should run only SSH and HTTPS. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Ignore the listener, because ports above 1024 cannot be exploited
Close port 443, because HTTPS is not needed on a web server
Restart nginx, because it is listening on an unexpected port
Investigate the python3 listener as a possible backdoor

explanation: An unexpected listener on port 4444 run by a python3 process does not belong to the approved services and may be a backdoor or reverse shell, so it needs investigation and containment. Port 443 is the required HTTPS service, and nginx is on its expected port. High-numbered ports are just as exploitable as low ones.

prompt: The ps output on a Linux server shows many processes in state Z, listed as <defunct>, all with the same parent process. What is the correct way to clear them?

options.text: Send SIGKILL to each defunct process until they are removed
Increase the server's swap space so defunct processes are paged out
Remount the root filesystem read-only to stop new defunct processes
Fix or restart the parent process so it reaps its child processes

explanation: Zombie (defunct) processes have already exited and only wait for their parent to collect their exit status, so the parent must reap them or be restarted, after which init adopts and reaps them. A zombie cannot be killed because it is not running. Swap and remounting filesystems have no effect on zombies.

prompt: An audit finds a Windows service named 'WinUpdateHelper' running from C:\Users\Public\svc.exe with automatic startup. No software installation records match it. What should the administrator treat this as?

options.text: A normal Windows Update component that should be left running
A rogue service that may be malware, requiring investigation and removal
A driver service that must stay to keep the server bootable
An orphaned service from a removed app that is safe to ignore

explanation: A service with a lookalike name running an executable from a public user folder, with no installation record, is a classic sign of a rogue service or persistence mechanism. Windows Update components run from system directories, not C:\Users\Public. Assuming it is harmless or orphaned skips needed investigation, and boot drivers do not run from user folders.

prompt: Security logs show a successful sign-in to a server's local administrator account at 03:12 from an IP address in another country. No administrator was working at that time. What should be done first?

options.text: Wait for the next sign-in from that IP address to confirm the pattern
Change the server's time zone so the sign-in falls in business hours
Treat it as unauthorized access and contain the account and server
Delete the security log so the event does not trigger further alerts

explanation: A successful administrator sign-in from an unexpected location and time indicates likely compromise, so the credentials should be revoked and the server contained while the incident is investigated. Waiting gives the attacker more time. Deleting logs destroys evidence, and changing the time zone hides nothing and fixes nothing.

prompt:
A file integrity monitoring tool reports the following on a Linux server:

changed: /usr/bin/ls  (SHA256 mismatch)
changed: /usr/bin/ps  (SHA256 mismatch)

No package updates were applied recently. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: System binaries were replaced, possibly by a rootkit hiding attacker activity
The files were defragmented, which changes their SHA256 hashes
The file integrity database is corrupted and should simply be reinitialized
The server's clock drifted, which changes the hash values of binaries

explanation: Changed hashes on tools like ls and ps without a matching package update suggest they were replaced, a common rootkit technique to hide files and processes; package verification such as rpm -V can confirm. Reinitializing the database would hide the evidence. Defragmentation and clock drift do not change file contents or their hashes.

prompt:
An administrator finds that a standard user on a Linux server was able to run commands as root. The command below shows an unusual result:

$ ls -l /usr/bin/find
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 204496 Nov 18 09:02 /usr/bin/find

What allowed the privilege escalation?

options.text: The setuid bit makes find run as root, and -exec runs commands as root
The find binary was modified recently, which grants temporary rights to users
The find binary is owned by root, which lets any user run every binary as root
The find binary is in /usr/bin, which the kernel runs with elevated privileges

explanation: The s in the owner execute position is the setuid bit, so find runs with root's effective identity for any user, and commands started through its -exec option inherit that identity; the bit should be removed. Root ownership alone does not make other users run a file as root. The directory a binary sits in and its modification date grant no privileges.

prompt: A data loss prevention (DLP) tool alerts that a server account uploaded a 4 GB archive containing customer records to an unapproved cloud storage site. What should the administrator do first?

options.text: Rename the archive on the server so it cannot be uploaded again
Block the transfer and suspend the account while investigating
Delete the DLP alert, because cloud storage uploads are normal for servers
Increase the DLP tool's size threshold so smaller uploads are not flagged

explanation: An unapproved upload of customer records is a potential data loss incident, so stopping further exfiltration and suspending the account come first, followed by investigation and any required notification. Dismissing or tuning away the alert ignores the incident. Renaming a file does not stop exfiltration through other paths.

prompt:
Users report that when they browse to the company's intranet site from one server, they reach a lookalike sign-in page instead. Other servers reach the real site. The administrator checks the affected server's hosts file and finds:

203.0.113.66   intranet.corp.example.com

What type of attack is this?

options.text: A distributed denial-of-service attack against the intranet
A privilege escalation through a setuid binary
Redirection through a tampered hosts file
A brute-force attack against the intranet's sign-in form

explanation: The hosts file entry overrides DNS and sends traffic for the intranet name to an attacker's address, a redirection attack used to harvest credentials. A DDoS overwhelms a service rather than redirecting clients. Brute force guesses passwords, and setuid escalation raises local privileges without redirecting traffic.

prompt: On a server subnet, the administrator runs arp -a on two servers and finds that the default gateway, 10.50.0.1, maps to the same MAC address as another server, 10.50.0.37. What is most likely happening?

options.text: The switch's VLAN configuration mirrors the gateway's MAC address
The gateway has failed over to 10.50.0.37 in a normal HA design
The two servers have stale ARP caches that will expire normally
ARP spoofing by 10.50.0.37 to intercept traffic

explanation: When the gateway's IP resolves to another host's MAC, that host has poisoned ARP caches so traffic flows through it, letting it intercept or alter data. Gateway redundancy uses a virtual IP and MAC, not an ordinary server's address. Stale caches would hold the old gateway MAC, and VLANs do not copy MAC addresses between hosts.

prompt: After cleaning up a compromised server, the administrator wants to reduce the chance of rogue services and open ports appearing again. Which three actions help? (Choose three.)

options.text: Allow anonymous SMB share access for convenience
Grant all administrators membership in every privileged group
Disable or remove services that are not needed
Review service accounts and remove unused ones
Close firewall ports not required by approved services

explanation: Removing unneeded services, closing unneeded ports and removing unused service accounts all shrink the attack surface. Putting every administrator in every privileged group violates least privilege. Anonymous share access gives unauthenticated users a foothold.
